culture/abbasid-caliphate.sum: The Abbasid Caliphate ruled much of the Islamic world from 750 CE, holding its court at Baghdad as a delta holds a river's gathered waters, until the Mongols sacked the city in 1258.

culture/aboriginal-australians.sum: Aboriginal Australians are the Indigenous peoples of the Australian mainland, whose ancestors arrived at least 50,000 years ago. Their cultures are among the oldest continuous living traditions, a fire carried unbroken from hand to hand…

culture/achaemenid-persians.sum: The Achaemenid Persians built the largest empire the world had yet seen, founded by Cyrus the Great about 550 BCE and standing until Alexander's conquest in 330 BCE, a realm that spread like dawn light across the old lands.

culture/al-andalus.sum: Al-Andalus was the Muslim-ruled part of the Iberian Peninsula from 711 to 1492, a region of Muslim, Christian and Jewish communities, three streams feeding one garden, that contributed to science, architecture and literature.

culture/ancestral-puebloans.sum: The Ancestral Puebloans raised large stone and cliff settlements across the American Southwest from about 700 to 1300 CE, among them the great houses of Chaco Canyon and the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde, until drought and hardship led…

culture/ancient-egyptians.sum: The ancient Egyptians built a state along the Nile that endured, with interruptions, for about three thousand years, as steady as the river's own return, until the Roman annexation in 30 BCE.

culture/ancient-greeks.sum: The ancient Greeks were a constellation of city-states around the Aegean and beyond, and their politics, philosophy and art shaped Mediterranean and later world culture as a spring shapes the valley below it.

culture/ayutthaya-kingdom.sum: The Ayutthaya Kingdom was a Tai state in central Thailand that lasted from 1351 to 1767 and grew into a major trading power, a harbor of many tongues where merchants from Asia and Europe were made welcome. It ended when Burmese armies…

culture/aztec-empire.sum: The Aztec (Mexica) Empire was a Triple Alliance of the cities of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan that dominated central Mexico from 1428 until the Spanish conquest in 1521. Think of it as an architecture of three pillars raised to hold…

culture/botai-culture.sum: The Botai culture was a society of hunter-herders in northern Kazakhstan, from roughly 3700 to 3100 BCE, who lived beside the horse and used it for meat, for milk, and probably for riding across the wind-scoured steppe.

culture/buddhism.sum: Buddhism began in northeastern India between the sixth and fourth centuries BCE, rising from the teaching of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, and it spread across Asia the way rivers spread across a delta, parting into several major…

culture/byzantine-empire.sum: The Byzantine Empire is the name given to the eastern Roman Empire, which burned on like a late lamp from the founding of Constantinople in 330 CE until the Ottoman conquest in 1453.

culture/casarabe-culture.sum: The Casarabe culture was a society of the Llanos de Mojos savanna in the Bolivian Amazon, active from about 500 to 1400 CE, whose monumental settlements were revealed by lidar in 2022, as if a veil had been drawn back from the land.

culture/celts.sum: The Celts were related peoples scattered across Iron Age Europe like embers from a shared hearth, bound by related languages and, later, by the La Tène style of art, yet never gathered into a single state. Rome absorbed most of the…

culture/champa.sum: Champa was a group of Cham states along the coast of central and southern Vietnam, dated from 192 CE, that built Hindu temples at My Son and sent its trade across the South China Sea like gulls over the water. Little by little it was…

culture/cherokee.sum: The Cherokee are a people native to the southeastern United States. Their nation adopted a written syllabary in the 1820s, survived the forced removal known as the Trail of Tears, and continues today as several federally recognized…

culture/chinchorro-culture.sum: The Chinchorro were fisher-hunter-gatherers of the Atacama Desert coast, in what is now northern Chile and southern Peru, known for the earliest deliberate artificial mummification, which began by about 5050 BCE on a shore between desert…

culture/chola-dynasty.sum: The Chola dynasty ruled much of southern India from around 850 to 1279 CE, a naval power whose ships traded and fought across the Bay of Bengal like hawks ranging over a wide field.

culture/christianity.sum: Christianity began among the followers of Jesus of Nazareth in first-century Roman Judea, and from that small spring it flowed out through the Mediterranean world until it became the most widely practiced religion in the world.

culture/confucianism.sum: Confucianism is a Chinese tradition of ethics and social order built on the teaching of Confucius (551 to 479 BCE). It became the official ideology of imperial China under the Han dynasty and shaped government and family life across East…

culture/daoism.sum: Daoism is a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition centered on living in harmony with the Dao, "the Way," as water lives in harmony with the slope it follows. It is traditionally traced to the sage Laozi, and in later ages it grew…

culture/delhi-sultanate.sum: The Delhi Sultanate was a succession of five Muslim dynasties that ruled much of northern India from 1206 until Babur's victory at Panipat in 1526, crowns passing from hand to hand like torches in a relay.

culture/franks.sum: The Franks were a Germanic people who moved into Roman Gaul like a river finding new ground, and there they raised one of early medieval Europe's most powerful kingdoms, first under the Merovingian dynasty of Clovis I and later under the…

culture/ghana-empire.sum: The Ghana Empire, called Wagadu by its own people, was a Soninke state in the western Sahel whose wealth rested on the trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt and ivory, carried over the sands like light over dark water. Its exact extent, its…

culture/gupta-empire.sum: The Gupta Empire ruled much of northern India from about 320 to 550 CE and is often associated with a flowering of mathematics, astronomy and the arts, a garden of the mind in full bloom.

culture/gokturk-khaganate.sum: The Göktürk Khaganate was a Turkic steppe empire, founded about 552 CE by Bumin Khagan, that spread across Inner Asia like wind over grass and left behind the earliest known Turkic writing.

culture/han-dynasty.sum: The Han dynasty ruled China from 206 BCE to 220 CE and set firm the imperial system begun under Qin, so that 'Han' is still the name of the majority ethnic group, a dynasty's name worn by a people.

culture/haudenosaunee-confederacy.sum: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy is a political union of Indigenous nations in the northeastern woodlands of North America, formed centuries before European contact, many strands braided into one cord.

culture/hinduism.sum: Hinduism is a family of religious traditions native to South Asia, grown out of the ancient Vedic religion the way a forest grows from old roots. It has no single founder or founding event, and today it counts about 1.2 billion adherents,…

culture/hittites.sum: The Hittites were a Bronze Age people of Anatolia who built an empire outward from their capital Hattusa, and the words on their lips were the earliest attested Indo-European language.

culture/inca-empire.sum: The Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu) was the largest state of the pre-Columbian Americas, ruling millions of people along the spine of the Andes from about 1438 until the Spanish conquest in 1533.

culture/indus-valley-civilization.sum: The Indus Valley Civilization (also called the Harappan) was a Bronze Age urban culture of the Indus River basin, at its height around 2600 to 1900 BCE, when its cities stood beside the river like ordered constellations.

culture/inuit-and-the-thule-expansion.sum: The Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, spread from Alaska across the Canadian Arctic to Greenland beginning around 1000 CE, moving over the ice like a tide, and replaced the earlier Dorset culture.

culture/islam.sum: Islam is the religion founded by Muhammad in seventh-century Arabia, centered on the Quran as the word of God and on the practices set out in its five pillars, and today, the way a spring becomes a river, it is the second-largest religion…

culture/jainism.sum: Jainism is an ancient Indian religion centered on non-violence toward all living things. It was taught by a line of teachers called tirthankaras and is traditionally traced to Mahavira in the sixth century BCE, though the tradition itself…

culture/jomon-culture.sum: The Jomon were hunter-gatherer-fishers of the Japanese archipelago who shaped some of the world's earliest pottery and lived in settled villages for about 14,000 years before rice farming arrived, a long and patient season among the…

culture/judaism.sum: Judaism is the religion and communal tradition of the Jewish people. It traces its origins to the patriarch Abraham and to the covenant given to Moses at Sinai, and for most of its history it has been organized around a body of law and…

culture/kalinago.sum: The Kalinago, called Caribs by Europeans, are an Indigenous people of the Lesser Antilles who resisted colonization for nearly two centuries after Columbus, and today they live mainly in the Kalinago Territory on Dominica. Theirs is a…

culture/kanem-bornu-empire.sum: Kanem-Bornu was a long-lived Muslim state around Lake Chad, governed by the Sayfawa dynasty, that survived by shifting its centre from Kanem to Bornu, as a river shifts its bed and flows on, and lasted until 1893.

culture/khmer-empire.sum: The Khmer Empire ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia from about 802 to 1431 CE, its capital at Angkor rising like a lotus from the waters.

culture/kingdom-of-aksum.sum: The Kingdom of Aksum was a trading empire in the highlands of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea, a crown set on high ground, from about the 1st to the 10th century CE.

culture/kingdom-of-benin.sum: The Kingdom of Benin was a West African forest state of the Edo people, ruled by an oba from Benin City, that flourished from about the 13th century until British forces conquered it in 1897. Its story shows how a kingdom builds its own…

culture/kingdom-of-kongo.sum: The Kingdom of Kongo was a centralized state in west-central Africa that adopted Catholic Christianity, dealt with Portugal as a diplomatic partner, and was drawn into the Atlantic slave trade. Think of it as an architecture of alliance…

culture/kingdom-of-kush.sum: The Kingdom of Kush was a Nubian state on the Nile south of Egypt, and its rulers came down the river like the season's flood, conquering Egypt and governing it as the 25th Dynasty (about 744 to 656 BCE).

culture/kingdom-of-mapungubwe.sum: Mapungubwe was an Iron Age trading state where the Limpopo and Shashe rivers meet in southern Africa, active from about the 11th to the 13th century, and its elite graves held gold and imported glass beads, light gathered from far shores…

culture/kingdom-of-saba.sum: Saba (Sheba) was an ancient South Arabian kingdom in what is now Yemen, centered on the city of Marib, and it grew rich on the incense trade, its wealth rising like fragrant smoke.

culture/kushan-empire.sum: The Kushan Empire, from about 30 to 375 CE, was a Central Asian empire that spanned Bactria and northern India like a bridge of kings, holding key Silk Road routes in its hands and patronizing Buddhism.

culture/lapita-culture.sum: The Lapita culture was a seafaring society that appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago around 1600 BCE and spread rapidly east through the western Pacific like light running along a wave, and its people were ancestors of the Polynesians.

culture/majapahit.sum: Majapahit was a Hindu-Buddhist empire based in eastern Java, founded in 1293 in the wake of the Yuan dynasty's failed invasion of Java, and in the 14th century it stood dominant over the Indonesian archipelago like a lamp over scattered…

culture/mal-ta-and-the-ancient-north-eur.sum: The Mal'ta boy, a child who lived near Lake Baikal about 24,000 years ago, carries a genome that revealed a previously unknown population, the 'Ancient North Eurasians', who contributed to the ancestry of both Europeans and Native…

culture/malacca-sultanate.sum: The Malacca (Melaka) Sultanate was a Malay port state on the Strait of Malacca, founded about 1400, a gate through which the sea's wealth poured. In the 15th century it became the leading trading port of Southeast Asia, and it helped…

culture/mali-empire.sum: The Mali Empire was a West African state, founded about 1235 by Sundiata Keita, that held the trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt in its grip, the sun-metal and the white treasure of the desert passing through its hands.

culture/manichaeism.sum: Manichaeism was a dualistic religion founded in third-century Persia by Mani, teaching a cosmic struggle between light and darkness. Within four centuries it had spread from North Africa to China like a lamp carried from hand to hand, and…

culture/maori.sum: The Maori are the Polynesian people of Aotearoa (New Zealand), who came ashore on the islands around 1250 to 1300 CE and grew there a distinct culture and language, as a seed carried over the sea takes root in new soil.

culture/mapuche.sum: The Mapuche are the Indigenous people of south-central Chile and Argentina, who resisted both the Inca and the Spanish and kept their independence for centuries. Think of their history as an architecture of refusal that held.

culture/marajoara-culture.sum: The Marajoara culture flourished on Marajo Island at the mouth of the Amazon, where the great river meets the sea, and it is known for large earthen mounds and richly decorated ceramics; its ceramic tradition is dated about 400 to 1300 CE.

culture/maurya-empire.sum: The Maurya Empire (322 to 185 BCE) was the first empire to unite most of the Indian subcontinent, gathering it the way a monsoon gathers rivers, and its capital stood at Pataliputra.

culture/maya.sum: The Maya are a group of Mesoamerican peoples who developed city-states, a full writing system, and an advanced astronomy that read the turning sky, and whose Classic period lasted about 250 to 900 CE.

culture/ming-dynasty.sum: The Ming dynasty ruled China from 1368 to 1644, rising like a new dawn after it expelled the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty.

culture/minoans.sum: The Minoans were a Bronze Age maritime civilization on the island of Crete, known for palaces such as Knossos and frescoes as vivid as sunlight on water. Their palatial culture flourished from about 2000 BCE until about 1450 BCE.

culture/mongol-empire.sum: The Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history, spread beneath a single sky; Genghis Khan founded it in 1206, and it later divided into four khanates.

culture/mughal-empire.sum: The Mughal Empire ruled much of the Indian subcontinent from 1526, when Babur won the Battle of Panipat, until 1857, when the British deposed the last emperor and the dynasty's long afternoon came to its end.

culture/muisca.sum: The Muisca were the peoples of the Colombian highlands around present-day Bogota, organized in a loose confederation of rulers, and their gold ritual inspired the legend of El Dorado. Their story is a study in how a ritual can be mistaken…

culture/mycenaean-greeks.sum: The Mycenaeans were the Bronze Age Greek-speaking civilization of mainland Greece, centered on palace-fortresses such as Mycenae, Tiryns, and Pylos that stood like eyries on the rock, from about 1600 to 1100 BCE.

culture/nabataeans.sum: The Nabataeans were an Arab people who controlled the caravan routes between Arabia and the Mediterranean from the 4th century BCE, building Petra and Hegra like cities dreamed in stone, until Rome annexed their kingdom in 106 CE.

culture/neo-assyrian-empire.sum: The Neo-Assyrian Empire, from about 911 to 609 BCE, was a large empire based in northern Mesopotamia, known for its army, its palace reliefs, and the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh. Hold those three together and you see its whole…

culture/norse.sum: The Norse (Vikings) were seafaring peoples from Scandinavia who raided, traded, and settled across Europe and the North Atlantic, riding the whale-road from about 793 to 1066 CE.

culture/olmecs.sum: The Olmecs were an early Mesoamerican culture on the Gulf coast of Mexico, best known for colossal carved stone heads that gaze out of deep time, from about 1200 to 400 BCE.

culture/ottoman-empire.sum: The Ottoman Empire was a state founded in Anatolia about 1299 that grew, like a great tree spreading its branches, into a multiethnic empire across Southeast Europe, West Asia, and North Africa, lasting until 1922.

culture/pagan-kingdom.sum: Under King Anawrahta and his successors, the Pagan Kingdom bound the Irrawaddy valley, in what is now Myanmar, into one realm, raised Theravada Buddhism as its state religion, and scattered thousands of temples across Bagan like seed…

culture/phoenicians.sum: The Phoenicians were seafaring traders from the city-states of the Levant coast, Tyre, Sidon and Byblos among them, who sowed colonies across the Mediterranean the way wind scatters seed along a shore.

culture/polynesians.sum: Polynesians are the Austronesian-speaking peoples of the central and eastern Pacific, who developed long-range voyaging and settled the islands strewn like thrown stars from Hawai'i to Aotearoa and Rapa Nui.

culture/qing-dynasty.sum: The Qing dynasty (1644 to 1912) was the last imperial dynasty of China, founded by the Manchus after they overthrew the Ming, and under it China's borders spread to their widest reach, like a tide at its highest mark.

culture/romans.sum: The Romans built a state that grew outward from the city of Rome like rings from a stone dropped in water, until it was an empire encircling the Mediterranean, and in the west it lasted until 476 CE.

culture/safavid-empire.sum: The Safavid Empire (1501 to 1736) was a Persian dynasty that made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Iran, ruling from Tabriz and later from Isfahan, its court carried like a lamp from one hall to another.

culture/scythians.sum: 'Scythian' is a broad name for the horse-riding nomads who moved like wind over grass across the Eurasian steppe in the Iron Age, from about the 9th to the 3rd century BCE; they are known from Greek writers and from rich burial mounds.

culture/shang-dynasty.sum: The Shang dynasty was the earliest Chinese dynasty with written records, ruling parts of the Yellow River region from about 1600 to 1046 BCE, the first voice of that land to reach us in its own hand.

culture/shinto.sum: Shinto is the indigenous religious tradition of Japan, gathered around kami, a broad category of spirits, deified ancestors and natural forces. It has no single founder and no single scripture, only a long history of local shrine practice,…

culture/sikhism.sum: Sikhism began in the Punjab region of South Asia with the teaching of Guru Nanak, born in 1469, and grew, as a tree grows ring by ring, through a line of ten human teachers into a monotheistic tradition with its own scripture and, since…

culture/sintashta-culture.sum: The Sintashta culture was a Bronze Age society of the southern Urals steppe, from about 2100 to 1800 BCE, known for fortified settlements ringed like the growth of a tree and for the earliest known spoke-wheeled chariots.

culture/sogdians.sum: The Sogdians were an Iranian-speaking people of the Central Asian oases (Samarkand, Bukhara, Panjikent) who, from about the 4th century CE, became the leading merchants of the Silk Roads, their caravans threaded across the continent like…

culture/sokoto-caliphate.sum: The Sokoto Caliphate was an Islamic state in what is now northern Nigeria, founded through the jihad of Usman dan Fodio from 1804, and in the 19th century it stood as the largest state in West Africa, spread like a great tree over the…

culture/song-dynasty.sum: The Song dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279 CE and presided over great advances in commerce, technology and urban life, an age when its cities burned bright as lanterns.

culture/songhai-empire.sum: The Songhai Empire was a West African state that followed Mali as the dominant power on the Niger River, from about 1464 until a Moroccan army defeated it in 1591, a reign that rose and fell like the river's flood.

culture/srivijaya.sum: Srivijaya was a Buddhist maritime kingdom seated at Palembang on Sumatra, and from the 7th to the 13th century it held the Strait of Malacca and its trade the way a hand holds a rope.

culture/sumerians.sum: The Sumerians were the people of southern Mesopotamia who built some of the world's first cities and developed cuneiform, the writing that first taught clay to remember.

culture/swahili-coast-city-states.sum: The Swahili city-states were trading towns strung along the East African coast like beads on a cord, Kilwa, Mombasa, and Lamu among them, and they flourished from about the 9th to the 15th century CE.

culture/taino.sum: The Taino were an Arawakan-speaking people of the Greater Antilles and the Bahamas, and in 1492 they became the first Indigenous Americans encountered by Columbus.

culture/tang-dynasty.sum: The Tang dynasty ruled China from 618 to 907 CE, and it is regarded as a high tide of Chinese poetry, art, and cosmopolitan culture.

culture/timurid-empire.sum: The Timurid Empire was a Turco-Mongol state founded by Timur in 1370; it ruled Central Asia and Iran from its capital at Samarkand, and it is remembered for its architecture and its science, as a garden is remembered for both its shade and…

culture/tokugawa-shogunate.sum: The Tokugawa shogunate was the military government that ruled Japan from 1603 to 1867, a long season of peace and of restricted foreign contact.

culture/umayyad-caliphate.sum: The Umayyad Caliphate ruled from Damascus from 661 to 750 CE, the first hereditary dynasty of Islamic rulers, and its reach ran like one long shoreline from Iberia to Sindh.

culture/xiongnu.sum: The Xiongnu were a confederation of steppe peoples bound together under Modu Shanyu in 209 BCE, a storm gathered on the grasslands that became the first great steppe empire and the chief rival of Han China.

culture/yakut-sakha.sum: The Sakha (Yakut) are a Turkic-speaking people of northeastern Siberia who developed horse and cattle herding in one of the coldest inhabited regions on Earth, where winter bites like iron. When they moved north is debated, but the…

culture/zagwe-dynasty.sum: The Zagwe dynasty ruled much of the Ethiopian highlands from about 1137 to 1270. Its best-known king, Lalibela, is remembered for a set of rock-hewn churches carved from living stone, prayers cut downward into the earth.

culture/zoroastrianism.sum: Zoroastrianism took its teaching from Zarathustra, an Iranian prophet, and set at its center the god Ahura Mazda and an unending contest between truth and the lie.

culture/zulu-kingdom.sum: From about 1816 the Zulu Kingdom rose under Shaka in southeastern Africa, and held its ground until the British triumph at Ulundi in 1879 broke its independence.

era/anthropocene.sum: The Anthropocene is a proposed geological interval, a name for the stretch of time in which human activity is the dominant influence on Earth's systems. Think of it as a signature we did not know we were signing. In March 2024 the…

era/archean-eon.sum: The Archean Eon, about 4.0 to 2.5 billion years ago, was the age in which the first continents stabilized like islands of cooling iron and life first appeared. Its air held almost no free oxygen, a sky still waiting for its breath.

era/bronze-age.sum: The Bronze Age, about 3300 to 1200 BCE in the Near East, was the age of bronze metallurgy, when copper met tin in the furnace, when the early states rose, and when the first writing was pressed into being.

era/cambrian-period.sum: The Cambrian Period, from 538.8 to 485.4 million years ago, is the first period of the Paleozoic Era, the dawn in which the seas put on armour. In its span most major animal body plans, and the first animals with hard parts, appear in the…

era/carboniferous-period.sum: The Carboniferous Period, from 358.9 to 298.9 million years ago, is the fifth period of the Paleozoic Era, and it bears the name of the coal its swamp forests laid down like black treasure in a vault. It is the age of the first amniote…

era/cenozoic-era.sum: The Cenozoic Era began 66 million years ago and has not yet ended; we stand inside it still. It is the age of mammals, of grasslands rolling to the horizon, of a climate slowly cooling, and within its span lies all of human history.

era/classical-antiquity.sum: Classical Antiquity, about 500 BCE to 500 CE, was the age of the great territorial empires, and of the philosophical and religious traditions that still shape the world like rivers running underground.

era/cretaceous-period.sum: The Cretaceous Period, from about 143.1 to 66 million years ago, is the last period of the Mesozoic Era and the longest of the Phanerozoic Eon. It was a warm greenhouse world in which the first flowering plants opened, and it ends as a…

era/cryogenian-period.sum: The Cryogenian Period, from 720 to 635 million years ago, is the middle period of the Neoproterozoic Era, and it is the time of the ice. Two global-scale glaciations. Ice. Then ice again. From them came the Snowball Earth hypothesis.

era/devonian-period.sum: The Devonian Period, from 419.2 to 358.9 million years ago, is the fourth period of the Paleozoic Era, often called the Age of Fishes. In its long span the first forests raised their crowns, the first limbed vertebrates came forth, and a…

era/early-modern-period.sum: The Early Modern Period, about 1500 to 1800 CE, is the era of oceanic exploration, global trade, the printing press, and the Scientific Revolution. Hold the other half of the ledger in the same hand: it is also the era of colonial empires…

era/ediacaran-period.sum: The Ediacaran Period, from 635 to 538.8 million years ago, is the last period of the Proterozoic Eon, the long dusk before the Cambrian dawn. In its span the first large, complex organisms rise into the fossil record like shapes surfacing…

era/epipaleolithic.sum: The Epipaleolithic is the final phase of the Paleolithic in the Near East and North Africa, from about 20,000 to about 10,000 BCE. It was the age of small composite stone tools, of foragers who began to linger in one place, and of the last…

era/hadean-eon.sum: The Hadean is the informal first eon of Earth's history, the age between the planet's forming, about 4.54 billion years ago, and roughly 4.0 billion years ago. Earth lay molten like ore in a crucible, then cooled as embers cool under ash,…

era/holocene-epoch.sum: The Holocene Epoch began about 11,700 years ago, as the last ice age loosened its grip, and it is the warm, relatively stable interval in which agriculture, cities and writing all arose, like seeds waking in a thawed field.

era/industrial-age.sum: The Industrial Age, about 1760 to 1945, is the era in which machines and fossil fuels transformed production, transport and warfare, and in which populations and cities grew rapidly. Think of it as the moment the architecture of human…

era/information-age.sum: The Information Age, from 1945 to the present, is the era of nuclear weapons, spaceflight, computers and the internet, and of the sharp rise in population and environmental impact known as the Great Acceleration. It is the age we still…

era/iron-age.sum: The Iron Age, about 1200 to 500 BCE and varying by region, was the age when iron tools and weapons spread across the lands like a grey tide, and new empires and belief systems rose.

era/jurassic-period.sum: The Jurassic Period, from 201.4 to about 143.1 million years ago, is the middle period of the Mesozoic Era, an age of giants and of early wings. In its span walked the largest land animals, the first known birds took form, and the Atlantic…

era/lower-paleolithic.sum: The Lower Paleolithic is the earliest part of the Paleolithic, from about 3.3 million to about 300,000 years ago, the age when stone first learned an edge. It holds the first stone tools, the long Acheulean handaxe tradition, and the…

era/medieval-period.sum: The Medieval or post-classical period, about 500 to 1500 CE, was the age when major world religions consolidated, when long-distance trade networks stretched like veins across the continents, and when large steppe and Islamic polities rose…

era/mesolithic.sum: The Mesolithic, the Middle Stone Age, is the period of hunter-gatherer societies that lived between the last ice age and the arrival of farming in Europe and neighbouring regions, from about 10,000 to about 5,000 BCE. Like shorelines, its…

era/mesoproterozoic-era.sum: The Mesoproterozoic Era is the middle era of the Proterozoic Eon, running from 1.6 billion to 1.0 billion years ago. It lies within the interval often called the "Boring Billion", a long hush in which climate, ocean chemistry and life…

era/mesozoic-era.sum: The Mesozoic Era, from 251.9 to 66 million years ago, is the age of dinosaurs, the long reign of the thunder-footed. Under its skies Pangaea broke apart, and the first flowering plants and the first mammals came into the world.

era/middle-paleolithic.sum: The Middle Paleolithic was the middle reach of the long Paleolithic, a span running from about 300,000 to about 50,000 years ago. It was the age of prepared-core stone tools, of the earliest Homo sapiens, and of several human species…

era/neogene-period.sum: The Neogene Period, from 23.03 to 2.58 million years ago, is the second period of the Cenozoic Era. In its span the grasslands spread outward, the climate cooled toward the ice ages, and the hominin lineage parted from that of the other…

era/neolithic.sum: The Neolithic is the age in which farming, animal herding, pottery and permanent villages took root in several parts of the world independently, like seeds no single hand had scattered, beginning about 11,500 years ago in Southwest Asia.

era/neoproterozoic-era.sum: The Neoproterozoic Era is the last era of the Proterozoic Eon, a long dusk running from 1.0 billion to 538.8 million years ago. In its keeping lie three great turnings: the supercontinent Rodinia breaking apart like ice on a spring river,…

era/ordovician-period.sum: The Ordovician Period, from 485.4 to 443.8 million years ago, is the second period of the Paleozoic Era, an age when the seas brimmed with new life. It saw a great rise in marine biodiversity, the first evidence of plants on land, and, at…

era/paleogene-period.sum: The Paleogene Period, from 66 to 23.03 million years ago, is the first period of the Cenozoic Era, a long morning after ruin. In it the mammals spread outward after the end-Cretaceous extinction, and the world turned from a warm, largely…

era/paleolithic.sum: The Paleolithic, the Old Stone Age, is the long era of chipped-stone tools and foraging societies, stretching like a road beneath changing skies from about 2.6 million years ago to the end of the last ice age.

era/paleoproterozoic-era.sum: The Paleoproterozoic Era is the first era of the Proterozoic Eon, running from 2.5 billion to 1.6 billion years ago. In it free oxygen first settled into the sky and stayed, a new voice in the air's old song, a lasting part of the…

era/paleozoic-era.sum: The Paleozoic Era (538.8 to 251.9 million years ago) was the age when animals first put on hard parts, when life crossed onto the land, when forests rose and the first tetrapods came. It ended in the largest mass extinction in Earth's…

era/permian-period.sum: The Permian Period, from 298.9 to 251.9 million years ago, is the last period of the Paleozoic Era, when the supercontinent Pangaea stood fully assembled, its lands gathered like fingers into one fist. Mammal-line reptiles ruled that great…

era/pleistocene-epoch.sum: The Pleistocene Epoch (about 2.58 million to 11,700 years ago) is the age of the returning ice, when great sheets advanced and withdrew again and again like a slow white tide. Beneath those shifting skies the genus Homo evolved and spread.

era/proterozoic-eon.sum: The Proterozoic Eon (2.5 billion to 538.8 million years ago) is the age of oxygenation, when the air first quickened; of complex cells; of global glaciations that gripped the world; and of the first multicellular animals.

era/quaternary-period.sum: The Quaternary Period is the latest period of the Cenozoic Era, begun 2.58 million years ago and still unfolding today. It is the age of the repeated ice ages, of the genus Homo, and of all recorded human history, every written word of it.

era/silurian-period.sum: The Silurian Period, from 443.8 to 419.2 million years ago, is the third period of the Paleozoic Era, a season of mending after the Late Ordovician extinction. In it rose the oldest known vascular land plants, and in its waters swam the…

era/tonian-period.sum: The Tonian Period is the first period of the Neoproterozoic Era, running from 1.0 billion to 720 million years ago. Its chronicle holds the break-up of the supercontinent Rodinia and the branching of eukaryotes into many kinds, a quiet…

era/triassic-period.sum: The Triassic Period, from 251.9 to 201.4 million years ago, is the first period of the Mesozoic Era, the long mending after the end-Permian extinction. In it the dinosaurs, the pterosaurs and the first mammals step for the first time onto…

era/upper-paleolithic.sum: The Upper Paleolithic was the last reach of the Paleolithic, from about 50,000 to about 10,000 BCE. It was the age of blade tools, of bone and antler worked into new shapes, of art and ornament scattered like seed, and of Homo sapiens…

event/1918-influenza-pandemic.sum: Between 1918 and 1920, an H1N1 virus swept the world as the influenza pandemic, infecting roughly a third of its people and taking an estimated 50 million lives.

event/abolition-of-slavery.sum: Between 1807 and 1888, first the transatlantic slave trade and then slavery itself were, one jurisdiction at a time, made illegal across the Atlantic world, closing out a system centuries old.

event/african-humid-period.sum: Green once, not always. From about 14,800 years ago to somewhere between 5,500 and 5,000, the Sahara held lakes. Rivers. Savanna. No desert — not yet. A stronger monsoon fed it all. Then the end. How it ended is debated. The marine cores…

event/age-of-revolutions.sum: Historians call the decades of political upheaval that swept around the Atlantic world, from the 1770s to the revolutions of 1848, the Age of Revolutions — though where its dates begin and end remains a matter of historians' choice; this…

event/alexander-s-conquests.sum: Between 336 and 323 BCE, Alexander III of Macedon overthrew the Achaemenid Persian Empire and stretched his rule from Greece and Egypt to the edge of India.

event/amazonian-urbanism-and-dark-earths.sum: Evidence gathers that the Amazon basin once held great, planned settlements — bound by roads and earthworks from about 500 BCE to the 1500s CE — and that its Indigenous peoples enriched the very soil and shape of the land.

event/american-civil-war.sum: From 1861 to 1865, the United States fought a civil war against eleven Southern states that seceded to form the Confederacy. Historians overwhelmingly agree that slavery stood at the center of secession itself. The war ended in Confederate…

event/american-revolution.sum: The American Revolution, fought from 1775 to 1783, was the war by which thirteen British colonies in North America became the independent United States.

event/animal-domestication.sum: In many lands, and each apart from the others, humankind tamed the wild into companionship. The dog came first, by at least 15,000 years ago, and the herds followed after — goats, sheep, pigs, and cattle, tamed from about 11,000 to 8,500…

event/armenian-genocide.sum: The Armenian Genocide was the deliberate destruction of most of the Ottoman Empire's Armenian population during World War I, carried out through mass killings, forced deportations, and death from starvation and exposure. Many countries and…

event/assembly-of-pangaea.sum: Nearly all the world's continents drew together into one land, Pangaea, mostly across the Carboniferous, about 335 to 300 million years ago — and held as one until it began to break apart about 200 million years ago.

event/assembly-of-rodinia.sum: Most of Earth's continental blocks drew together into one land, Rodinia, between about 1.3 and 0.9 billion years ago. Its shape is read from mountain belts and the magnetic memory of old rock, and how its pieces were arranged is still…

event/atlantic-slave-trade.sum: Between the early 16th and the mid-19th centuries, the transatlantic slave trade forcibly transported about 12.5 million Africans to the Americas, and millions did not survive the passage.

event/austronesian-expansion.sum: Beginning roughly 5,000 to 5,500 years ago, speakers of Austronesian languages spread outward from Taiwan like ripples from a stone dropped in still water, until at last their words touched Madagascar in the west and Rapa Nui in the east.

event/axial-age.sum: The 'Axial Age' is the name given to the span of roughly 800 to 200 BCE, when major philosophical and religious traditions rose like separate springs across Eurasia, in China, India, Persia, Israel, and Greece.

event/banded-iron-formations.sum: Banded iron formations are ancient sedimentary rocks striped like the pages of a closed book, iron-rich layers alternating with silica-rich ones, laid down mostly between about 3.8 and 1.8 billion years ago. They are a major source of the…

event/bantu-expansion.sum: Over about four thousand years, Bantu-speaking peoples spread from a homeland in West-Central Africa (present-day Nigeria and Cameroon) across central, eastern, and southern Africa, the way a river in flood spreads across a plain.

event/battle-of-adwa.sum: On 1 March 1896, at the Battle of Adwa, the Ethiopian army under Emperor Menelik II decisively defeated an invading Italian force, and with that victory secured Ethiopia's independence.

event/battle-of-kadesh.sum: The Battle of Kadesh, fought around 1274 BCE near the Orontes River in what is now Syria, set Ramesses II of Egypt against Muwatalli II of the Hittite Empire in one of the largest chariot battles on record.

event/battle-of-talas.sum: In 751 CE, near the Talas River in present-day Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan, a Tang Chinese army met an Abbasid army at the Battle of Talas, and the encounter ended in Tang defeat.

event/bengal-famine-of-1943.sum: The Bengal famine of 1943 killed an estimated 2 to 3 million people in British-ruled Bengal during World War II. Historians debate its causes, yet they agree on two things: it was not simply a shortage of food, and wartime policy played a…

event/black-death.sum: The Black Death was a plague pandemic caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. From 1346 to 1353 it swept through Eurasia and North Africa. Town after town. Road after road.

event/boxer-rebellion.sum: The Boxer Rebellion (1899 to 1901) was an anti-foreign, anti-Christian uprising in northern China, backed by the Qing court, and it ended in defeat at the hands of an eight-nation alliance.

event/breakup-of-pangaea.sum: Pangaea, the supercontinent that had gathered itself together by about 300 million years ago, began to split about 200 million years ago, and through the widening seam the Atlantic Ocean opened and the map of the world was remade.

event/british-raj.sum: The British Raj was the period of direct British rule over the Indian subcontinent, from 1858 to 1947. It opened when the Crown took over from the East India Company after the Rebellion of 1857, and it closed with the independence and…

event/bronze-age-collapse.sum: Around 1200 BCE, the eastern Mediterranean and the Near East came apart. State after state, within a few decades. The palace economies of the Late Bronze Age did not slow. They stopped.

event/blling-allerd-warming.sum: The world warmed like a held breath released: the Bølling-Allerød was an abrupt warm interval that began about 14,700 years ago and lasted until about 12,900 years ago, the first great thaw after the Last Glacial Maximum. It ended as…

event/cambrian-explosion.sum: In a span the fossil record reads as a heartbeat, roughly 13 to 25 million years beginning 538.8 million years ago, the Cambrian Explosion brought forth most of the major animal body plans that would ever appear.

event/campanian-ignimbrite-eruption.sum: Near Naples, Italy, the Campi Flegrei caldera let go. About 39,850 years ago. The Campanian Ignimbrite eruption — the largest explosive blast Europe had seen in roughly the last 200,000 years. Its ash reached the Mediterranean. It reached…

event/carboniferous-coal-forests.sum: In the wet tropical lowlands of the later Carboniferous, roughly 323 to 299 million years ago, swamp forests rose and rotted and rose again, and their buried remains became much of the world's coal.

event/chinese-reform-and-opening.sum: Beginning in December 1978, China under Deng Xiaoping rewrote the architecture of its economy: market reforms went in, foreign trade opened up, and across the following decades growth compounded at a pace the world had rarely seen.

event/classic-maya-collapse.sum: Between about 800 and 950 CE, one city after another in the southern Maya lowlands stopped raising monuments. Some were abandoned outright. Elsewhere, Maya communities went on.

event/closure-of-the-isthmus-of-panama.sum: A slender bridge of land rose between two continents: the Isthmus of Panama, traditionally dated to about 3 million years ago, joined North and South America, sealed the sea-road between the Pacific and the Atlantic, and set loose a great…

event/cold-war.sum: The Cold War, about 1947 to 1991, was a global rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies — fought mainly through arms races, alliances, and proxy wars rather than direct battle.

event/collapse-of-the-soviet-union.sum: The Soviet Union dissolved on 26 December 1991, following the revolutions of 1989 across Eastern Europe and a failed coup in August 1991 — and with it, the Cold War ended.

event/collision-of-india-and-asia.sum: Beginning about 50 million years ago, the Indian plate met Eurasia in a slow collision that raised the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau — a convergence that continues even now.

event/colonization-of-land.sum: Life's move onto land was a slow migration in stages: plants first, then arthropods and vertebrates, beginning about 470 million years ago, and the surface of the planet was transformed in the process.

event/columbian-exchange.sum: The Columbian Exchange names the transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world, beginning after 1492.

event/congo-free-state.sum: From 1885 to 1908, the Congo Free State was a vast territory in Central Africa held as the personal possession of King Leopold II of Belgium — a rule notorious for forced labor in rubber and ivory collection and for mass deaths.

event/control-of-fire.sum: Somewhere near a million years past, the ancestors of this species first bent flame to their will, and by about 400,000 years ago the keeping of fire had become habit, not marvel.

event/covid-19-pandemic.sum: The COVID-19 pandemic was a global outbreak of the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, first identified in late 2019.

event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction.sum: About 66 million years ago, a rock fell on what is now Mexico. The Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction followed. Every non-avian dinosaur, gone. About three-quarters of all species with them.

event/crusades.sum: The Crusades were a series of religiously sanctioned military expeditions, launched by Western European Christians from 1095, largely to capture and hold Jerusalem and other holy sites in the Levant.

event/deccan-traps-eruptions.sum: Lava poured across west-central India. Huge. The main phases of the Deccan Traps eruptions: about 66.3 to 65.5 million years ago. They overlap the end-Cretaceous extinction. What role they played in it is still debated.

event/decolonization.sum: Decolonization was the process by which most colonies of European empires became independent states, largely between 1945 and 1975.

event/devonian-forests-and-the-rise-of-t.sum: The Devonian forests were the first forests Earth ever wore, rising about 385 million years ago and spreading like a slow green tide through the rest of the period. Trees were not born once but again and again, in several plant lineages…

event/digital-revolution.sum: The Digital Revolution is the spread of digital computing and networks from the mid-20th century on, and it includes the internet (from 1969) and the World Wide Web (from 1989 to 1991). Think of it as a new architecture of connection laid…

event/divergence-of-the-hominin-lineage.sum: The hominin lineage, the line that leads to humans, parted from the line leading to chimpanzees and bonobos between roughly 6 and 8 million years ago in Africa, as one river divides around a stone into two streams.

event/domestication-of-maize.sum: Maize, or corn, was coaxed from a wild grass called teosinte in southwestern Mexico about 9,000 years ago, and from that small beginning it grew into a staple crop across the Americas, as a spring swells into a river.

event/domestication-of-rice.sum: Rice (Oryza sativa) was drawn out of wild rice in the Yangtze River region of China beginning around 9,000 to 7,000 years ago, not in a single stroke but over a long process, slow as silt settling in a river's bend.

event/domestication-of-the-dog.sum: Dogs descend from a now-extinct population of Pleistocene wolves, a people of the ice long gone from the world, yet when and where the taming happened is one of the most disputed dates in the whole domestication record. Genetic studies set…

event/dutch-east-india-company.sum: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) was a chartered trading company founded in 1602 with a monopoly on Dutch trade in Asia, and it stands among the first companies to issue tradable shares. Notice the pairing: a state's charter on one side,…

event/earliest-continental-crust.sum: The earliest continental crust was the young world's first raft of stone light enough to ride above the sea — a granite-kin skin, buoyant against the ocean floor's darker basalt. It may have formed before 4.0 billion years ago, but the…

event/early-hominin-dispersals-from-afri.sum: Hominins first stepped beyond Africa's borders between about 2.1 and 1.8 million years ago, and in the million years that followed they spread across Eurasia in wave after wave. The oldest hominin bones found outside Africa lie at Dmanisi…

event/emergence-of-symbolic-art.sum: Symbolic behavior — ochre carved with pattern, beads strung and worn, paintings laid on stone — enters the record of the deep past from about 100,000 years onward, like the first faint light before a long dawn.

event/emergence-of-the-genus-homo.sum: In East Africa, between about 2.8 and 1.8 million years ago, the genus Homo rose from an ancestor built in the mold of Australopithecus. The oldest fossil claimed for Homo is a broken jaw from Ledi-Geraru, Ethiopia, some 2.8 million years…

event/enlightenment.sum: The Enlightenment names an architecture of thought: an 18th-century movement across Europe that placed reason, evidence, and individual rights above inherited authority, and challenged that authority at its root.

event/eocene-oligocene-transition.sum: The Eocene-Oligocene transition was a swift chilling of the whole Earth, about 34 million years ago, when ice took hold on Antarctica and did not let go. It marks the turning point where a warm, greenhouse world began its long slide toward…

event/fall-of-constantinople.sum: On 29 May 1453, Ottoman forces under Sultan Mehmed II took Constantinople after a siege of about eight weeks, closing the ledger on the Byzantine Empire.

event/fall-of-the-western-roman-empire.sum: The Western Roman Empire came to its end in 476 CE, when the Germanic general Odoacer cast down Romulus Augustulus, the last emperor to rule in the west.

event/first-fleet-and-the-colonization-o.sum: In January 1788, eleven British ships — the First Fleet — reached Botany Bay carrying about 1,400 people, roughly half of them convicts, and from this beginning the colony of New South Wales was founded at Sydney Cove.

event/fish-to-tetrapod-transition.sum: The Fish-to-Tetrapod Transition was the slow reshaping of fin into limb — four-limbed creatures rising from lobe-finned fishes across the Middle and Late Devonian, roughly 385 to 360 million years ago. The unfolding sequence is well…

event/formation-of-the-oceans.sum: The Formation of the Oceans marks the time, probably between about 4.4 and 4.0 billion years ago, when liquid water first gathered on the face of the cooling young Earth. The date itself is uncertain, resting only on evidence read at a…

event/formation-of-the-solar-system-and-.sum: The Solar System was born about 4.57 billion years ago, out of a cloud of gas and dust collapsing upon itself, and Earth gathered from that same material over tens of millions of years.

event/french-revolution.sum: The French Revolution, from 1789 to 1799, overturned the monarchy in France, declared the rights of man and citizen, and opened the path to the rise of Napoleon Bonaparte.

event/genomic-revolution.sum: The Genomic Revolution began with the identification of the DNA double helix in 1953, and it has since made it possible to read, and to edit, the genetic code of living things.

event/great-acceleration.sum: The Great Acceleration names the sharp, simultaneous rise, since about 1950, in human population, energy use, economic output, and environmental change.

event/great-ordovician-biodiversificatio.sum: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification was a long flowering of life in the seas, a rise in the diversity of marine animals running from about 485 to 460 million years ago, which multiplied the species and families held within body plans…

event/great-oxidation-event.sum: The Great Oxidation Event was the rise of free oxygen into Earth's air, beginning about 2.4 billion years ago, driven by the quiet work of photosynthetic microbes.

event/green-revolution.sum: The Green Revolution was the spread, from the 1940s to the 1970s, of high-yield crop varieties, fertilizers, and irrigation, and it greatly increased grain production.

event/haitian-revolution.sum: The Haitian Revolution, from 1791 to 1804, was a rebellion of enslaved people against the French colony of Saint-Domingue, and it created the independent state of Haiti.

event/holocaust.sum: The Holocaust was the persecution of European Jews by Nazi Germany beginning in 1933, and the systematic murder of about six million of them from 1941 to 1945, carried out with the help of allies and collaborators.

event/huronian-glaciation.sum: Ice came. Then it came again. The Huronian Supergroup of Ontario, Canada, holds a series of ice ages from the early Paleoproterozoic, about 2.4 to 2.2 billion years ago. One of the oldest ice ages we can still read clearly in stone.

event/incense-trade.sum: The incense trade carried frankincense and myrrh out of southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, across desert and season, to Mediterranean and Mesopotamian markets — borne mostly on camel caravan, for well over a thousand years.

event/indian-ocean-trade-network.sum: The Indian Ocean trade network was a web of sea routes binding East Africa, Arabia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and China together, and it ran busiest from about the 8th to the 15th century CE.

event/indian-rebellion-of-1857.sum: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 began as a mutiny of sepoys, the Indian soldiers of the East India Company army, at Meerut on 10 May 1857, and it grew into a wider uprising across northern and central India that ended British East India…

event/indian-removal-and-the-trail-of-te.sum: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 authorized the United States to relocate Native American nations from the southeastern states to lands west of the Mississippi, and it led to the forced marches known as the Trail of Tears. Notice the shape…

event/indo-european-language-spread.sum: The languages of the Indo-European family, among them the ancestors of English, Hindi, Persian, Greek, Latin, and Russian, spread across Eurasia beginning several thousand years ago, like one river breaking into many channels across a vast…

event/industrial-revolution.sum: The Industrial Revolution was the shift, beginning in Britain about 1760, from hand production and animal power to machine production driven by coal and steam. Picture the hand at the loom and the horse at the wheel, and then picture both…

event/interbreeding-of-homo-sapiens-with.sum: Homo sapiens interbred with Neanderthals and with Denisovans, as ancient and present-day DNA show, three branches of one old tree folding back into one another. Most people outside Africa carry about 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal ancestry,…

event/invention-of-writing.sum: Writing was invented independently at least three or four times, kindled first in Mesopotamia about 3400 to 3200 BCE as a way to record goods and obligations, and like fire it was struck anew in lands that never saw the first spark.

event/last-glacial-maximum.sum: The Last Glacial Maximum was the latest hour in which the world's ice sheets stood at their widest reach, a cold and lasting reign that held from about 26,500 to 19,000 years ago.

event/late-devonian-extinction.sum: The Late Devonian extinction was no single blow. Over a long, grinding stretch — about 372 to 359 million years ago — life in the seas thinned out. The reef builders took the worst of it.

event/late-heavy-bombardment.sum: The Late Heavy Bombardment: a hypothesized spike, asteroids battering the inner Solar System, roughly 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago. The evidence comes mostly from lunar rock — radiometric ages, read like scars.

event/late-ordovician-extinction.sum: The Late Ordovician extinction — about 445 to 443 million years ago — was first. First of the 'Big Five.' It erased an estimated 85 to 86 percent of species, most of them from the sea.

event/latin-american-wars-of-independenc.sum: Between about 1808 and 1826, the Latin American wars of independence dismantled Spanish rule across most of the Americas and raised in its place a series of new republics.

event/manila-galleon-trade.sum: From 1565 to 1815, Spanish galleons crossed each year between Manila and Acapulco, carrying Chinese goods to the Americas and American silver to Asia — the first regular trans-Pacific trade the world had seen.

event/meiji-restoration.sum: The Meiji Restoration was Japan's political and social transformation: it followed the arrival of American warships in 1853, ended the Tokugawa shogunate in 1868, and opened an era of rapid industrialization.

event/messinian-salinity-crisis.sum: The Messinian Salinity Crisis names an age, from about 5.96 to 5.33 million years ago, when the Mediterranean Sea was severed from the Atlantic and, in its long isolation, laid down thick salt upon its floor.

event/mexican-revolution.sum: The Mexican Revolution, from 1910 to 1920, overthrew the long rule of Porfirio Díaz and moved through a series of civil wars among revolutionary leaders before producing the Constitution of 1917. Its death toll is uncertain, but is usually…

event/mfecane.sum: The Mfecane — 'the crushing' — names a period of upheaval, warfare, and migration across southern Africa in the early 19th century, associated with the rise of the Zulu Kingdom.

event/middle-pleistocene-transition.sum: The rhythm broke. Between about 1.25 million and 0.7 million years ago, the ice ages changed their beat. Cycles stretched — from about 41,000 years to about 100,000 — and the ice grew larger, the cold grew worse.

event/milankovitch-cycles-and-the-ice-ag.sum: Milankovitch cycles: slow, regular changes — the shape of Earth's orbit, the tilt of its axis, the wobble in that tilt. They shift how sunlight falls, by latitude, by season. And since about 2.6 million years ago, they have set the beat…

event/miocene-great-ape-radiation.sum: The Miocene great ape radiation was the flowering of apes across Africa, Europe, and Asia, between about 23 and 7 million years ago — a time when many more kinds of ape walked the earth than remain today.

event/modern-climate-change.sum: Modern climate change is the warming of Earth, caused mainly by human emissions of greenhouse gases, most of them from the burning of fossil fuels.

event/mongol-conquests.sum: From 1206 onward, the Mongols, under Genghis Khan and those who followed him, built the largest contiguous land empire history has known, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe.

event/moon-landing.sum: On 20 July 1969, the Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above them — the first time humans had stood on another world.

event/napoleonic-wars.sum: The Napoleonic Wars, from 1803 to 1815, were fought between Napoleon's French Empire and shifting coalitions of European powers, and ended in his defeat at Waterloo.

event/neanderthal-extinction.sum: Gone. Neanderthals vanished from Europe's archaeological record about 41,000 to 39,000 years ago, according to radiocarbon dating at 40 sites. Thousands of years of overlap with Homo sapiens came first. No single cause is agreed.

event/nuclear-age.sum: The Nuclear Age began on 16 July 1945, with the first test of a nuclear weapon, followed by the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August.

event/onset-of-northern-hemisphere-glaci.sum: Ice grew. Large sheets, across North America and Eurasia, about 2.7 million years ago. And with that growth began the repeating glacial and interglacial cycles of the Quaternary Period.

event/onset-of-plate-tectonics.sum: The onset of plate tectonics marks the hour when the rigid plates of Earth's outer shell began their slow march, the ocean floor swallowed back into the mantle at the subduction zones. Proposed dates range from before 4 billion to about…

event/opening-of-the-silk-roads.sum: The Silk Roads were braided threads of road and sea, linking East Asia, South Asia, Central Asia, and the Mediterranean, growing from the second century BCE onward.

event/opium-wars.sum: The Opium Wars were two conflicts between Qing China and Britain — joined, in the second, by France — fought over trade and diplomatic relations, from 1839 to 1842 and from 1856 to 1860, and they opened China to Western commerce on unequal…

event/origin-of-bipedalism.sum: Habitual upright walking rose in the human lineage, in Africa, somewhere between roughly 7 and 4 million years ago — the earliest mark of the hominins, older by millions of years than large brains or the first stone tools, though its true…

event/origin-of-birds.sum: From small, feathered theropod dinosaurs of the Jurassic came the birds, first known in fossils about 160 to 150 million years old, sparks struck from a long dynasty of scaled kin. Of all the dinosaur lines, only this one still lives,…

event/origin-of-eukaryotes.sum: Eukaryotes, cells bearing a nucleus and inner organelles, the stuff from which every animal, plant and fungus is built, arose roughly 2 billion years ago, though the date carries very wide uncertainty.

event/origin-of-homo-sapiens.sum: Anatomically modern humans, Homo sapiens, took shape across Africa by about 300,000 years ago, not at a single hearth, but through a gradual process spanning the continent.

event/origin-of-language.sum: When spoken language began, no one knows, because neither speech nor the brain's grammar circuitry leaves a fossil. The published estimates for when the capacity existed range from about 2 million to 50,000 years ago, depending on whether…

event/origin-of-life.sum: Life on Earth rose up at least 3.5 billion years ago, and perhaps earlier still. How it began, no one yet knows.

event/origin-of-mammals.sum: Mammals rose slowly from the mammal-line reptiles called synapsids, and the oldest candidates for the name come from the Late Triassic, roughly 225 to 205 million years past, though the very date bends on how one defines a mammal.

event/origin-of-multicellularity.sum: Multicellularity, in which cells cling together, divide their labor, and reproduce as one body, arose independently again and again. The clearest early fossil evidence stands about 1.05 billion years old, and the older claims remain…

event/origin-of-photosynthesis.sum: Photosynthesis, the trick of turning light into the making of organic molecules, rose among bacteria sometime in the Archean, perhaps as early as 3.5 billion years ago. The date of the first oxygen-producing form stays uncertain and…

event/out-of-africa-dispersal.sum: Homo sapiens spread out of Africa and across the whole world. Genetic studies trace most of today's non-African ancestry to one major dispersal, roughly 70,000 to 50,000 years ago, though earlier and smaller dispersals left their own…

event/paleocene-eocene-thermal-maximum.sum: The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum was a burst of global warming about 56 million years ago, when a great release of carbon drove global temperatures up by roughly 5 to 6 degrees Celsius, and held them there for about 200,000 years.

event/partition-of-india.sum: In August 1947, British India was divided into the two independent states of India and Pakistan, and the new borders drawn through Punjab and Bengal set off mass migration and violence.

event/peace-of-westphalia.sum: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 was made up of the treaties of Osnabruck and Munster, which brought an end to both the Thirty Years' War and the Eighty Years' War between Spain and the Dutch Republic.

event/peopling-of-europe-by-homo-sapiens.sum: Homo sapiens reached Europe by about 45,000 years ago, and perhaps earlier still, stepping into a continent already held by the Neanderthals. The earliest securely dated remains, from Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria and from Ranis in Germany,…

event/peopling-of-sahul.sum: Modern humans reached Sahul, the Pleistocene landmass that joined Australia to New Guinea, at least 50,000 years ago, and perhaps about 65,000 years ago.

event/peopling-of-southeast-asia-and-wal.sum: Homo sapiens reached mainland Southeast Asia by about 86,000 to 68,000 years ago, and the Wallacean islands beyond it, Sulawesi and Timor among them, by about 51,000 to 42,000 years ago. This dispersal supplied both the route and the rough…

event/peopling-of-the-americas.sum: Humans reached the Americas out of northeastern Asia by at least 15,000 years ago, and perhaps much earlier still. The earliest date remains contested.

event/permian-triassic-extinction.sum: The Permian-Triassic extinction, about 251.9 million years ago, was the largest mass extinction in Earth's history. It killed an estimated 80 to 96 percent of marine species. Eight in ten, at the least. Nearly all, at the worst. Gone.

event/polynesian-settlement-of-the-pacif.sum: Polynesian navigators settled the last remote islands of the central and eastern Pacific, reaching their furthest point with Aotearoa New Zealand around 1250 to 1300 CE.

event/portuguese-sea-route-to-india.sum: Vasco da Gama's fleet made landfall at Calicut in India on 20 May 1498, having sailed clear around Africa, and so opened a direct sea road from Europe to Asia.

event/protestant-reformation.sum: The Protestant Reformation began in 1517, when Martin Luther publicized his Ninety-five Theses against the practices of the church, and it split Western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant churches.

event/quaternary-megafauna-extinctions.sum: Between roughly 50,000 and 10,000 years ago, the biggest animals on land began to vanish. A large share of them. The timing differed by continent. Often, the disappearances followed close on the arrival of humans.

event/radiation-of-placental-mammals.sum: After the end-Cretaceous extinction, the placental mammals radiated fast. From about 66 to 50 million years ago, they filled every space left empty. Most living mammals belong to that radiation.

event/renaissance.sum: The Renaissance was a movement of art, learning and political thought, born in Italian city-states such as Florence in the 14th and 15th centuries and spreading from there across all of Europe.

event/rise-of-islam.sum: Islam emerged in Arabia beginning in 610 CE, and within about a century it had spread, through conquest and through conversion, across territory reaching from Iberia to Central Asia.

event/russian-expansion-into-siberia.sum: Between 1582 and 1639, Russian Cossacks and traders pushed across Siberia all the way to the Pacific, driven by the fur trade and by the tribute, yasak, taken from Indigenous peoples.

event/russian-revolution.sum: The Russian Revolution of 1917 overthrew the Tsarist monarchy, and the Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin then seized power in turn, leading on to a civil war and to the formation of the Soviet Union in 1922.

event/scientific-revolution.sum: The Scientific Revolution was the shift, roughly from 1543 to 1687, toward systematic experiment, mathematics and observation as the basis for knowledge of nature, centered in Europe.

event/scramble-for-africa.sum: The Scramble for Africa was the rapid partition of the African continent among European powers between about 1881 and 1914, in which the share of Africa under European control rose from roughly 10 percent to about 90 percent.

event/second-italo-ethiopian-war.sum: Between October 1935 and May 1936, Italy's colonial invasion of Ethiopia unfolded as a stark violation of the architecture of collective security: Italian forces used mustard gas, seized the capital, and drove Emperor Haile Selassie into…

event/second-sino-japanese-war.sum: The Second Sino-Japanese War (1937 to 1945) was the full-scale war between Japan and China that opened at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing and later merged into World War II. Its violence included the mass killing of civilians, among…

event/seven-years-war.sum: The Seven Years' War (1756 to 1763) was fought between Britain and France, and their allies, across several continents, and it left Britain dominant in both North America and India.

event/siberian-traps-eruptions.sum: The Siberian Traps eruptions: one of the largest volcanic outpourings of the last 500 million years. Northern Siberia, about 252 to 251 million years ago. They coincide with the end-Permian mass extinction.

event/snowball-earth.sum: Snowball Earth: glaciations in the late Proterozoic. The Sturtian and the Marinoan, roughly 717 to 635 million years ago. Ice, perhaps, reaching all the way to the tropics.

event/space-age.sum: The Space Age opened on 4 October 1957, when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite.

event/spanish-conquest-of-the-aztec-empi.sum: Between 1519 and 1521, a small Spanish force under Hernan Cortes — allied with many Indigenous city-states and aided by epidemic disease — overthrew the Aztec Empire and captured Tenochtitlan.

event/spanish-conquest-of-the-inca-empir.sum: In 1532, Francisco Pizarro's small Spanish force captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, opening a conquest of the Inca Empire that ended with the fall of the last Inca stronghold in 1572.

event/spread-of-grasslands.sum: Across the Miocene, from about 25 to 5 million years ago, open grasslands spread like a green tide across the continents. Animal life was remade in its wake, and the plant family that advanced with it now supplies most of the world's…

event/suez-canal.sum: The Suez Canal, opened on 17 November 1869, is a sea-level waterway across Egypt linking the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, shortening the sea route between Europe and Asia.

event/sugar-plantation-complex.sum: From the 1500s, European colonizers built large sugar plantations across Brazil and the Caribbean, worked mainly by enslaved Africans — one of the most profitable and brutal systems in early modern trade.

event/taiping-rebellion.sum: The Taiping Rebellion (1850 to 1864) was a civil war in Qing China led by Hong Xiuquan, who claimed to be the younger brother of Jesus Christ; it stands among the deadliest conflicts in history.

event/tanzimat-reforms.sum: The Tanzimat (Reorganization) was a series of reforms in the Ottoman Empire between 1839 and 1876 that sought to modernize the state, promise equality before the law to all subjects, and move it toward constitutional government.

event/the-agricultural-revolution.sum: The Agricultural Revolution was the slow turning, beginning about 11,500 years ago, from the forager's wandering path to the farmer's rooted one — a shift toward tending crops and herds that arose, like scattered fires catching…

event/the-boring-billion.sum: The Boring Billion: an informal name for the stretch from about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago. No well-established ice ages. Little apparent change in the fossil record. Silence, on the surface. Whether it was truly uneventful — still…

event/the-urban-revolution.sum: The Urban Revolution was the rising of the first true cities, beginning around 3500 BCE in southern Mesopotamia — places dense with people, threaded with specialized labor, and bound by central institutions.

event/theia-impact-and-the-formation-of-.sum: According to the giant-impact hypothesis, a Mars-sized body called Theia struck the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago. Out of the wreckage: the Moon.

event/thirty-years-war.sum: The Thirty Years' War (1618 to 1648) was a set of linked wars across central Europe, begun as a religious conflict within the Holy Roman Empire and ended by the Peace of Westphalia.

event/toba-eruption.sum: The Toba eruption: about 74,000 years ago, in Sumatra. One of the largest volcanic eruptions of the past two million years. Its effects on human populations — still debated.

event/translation-movement-and-the-house.sum: From the mid-8th to the 10th century, scholars in Abbasid Baghdad gathered the words of distant tongues — Greek, Persian, Syriac, Indian — and turned them into Arabic, then carried the ideas further still.

event/treaty-of-waitangi.sum: The Treaty of Waitangi, first signed on 6 February 1840, stands as the founding agreement between the British Crown and many Maori chiefs of Aotearoa New Zealand.

event/triassic-jurassic-extinction.sum: The Triassic-Jurassic extinction. About 201.4 million years ago. A large share of marine and land species: gone. Space cleared for the rise of the dinosaurs.

event/tunguska-event.sum: The Tunguska event was an explosion in the atmosphere above the Podkamennaya Tunguska River in Siberia, on 30 June 1908, which flattened about 2,000 square kilometers of forest.

event/turkish-war-of-independence.sum: The Turkish War of Independence (1919 to 1923) was fought by a nationalist movement under Mustafa Kemal against the Allied occupation of Anatolia and the invading armies of Greece and Armenia, ending the Ottoman sultanate and establishing…

event/unification-of-china-under-qin.sum: In 221 BCE, the state of Qin conquered its rivals and forged the first unified Chinese empire under Qin Shi Huang.

event/unification-of-egypt.sum: Upper and Lower Egypt were joined into a single state around 3100 BCE, traditionally by a ruler named Narmer, or Menes.

event/vedic-period.sum: The Vedic period, roughly 1500 to 500 BCE, was the age in which the Vedas were composed — the oldest Indian sacred texts, given voice in the Sanskrit language.

event/women-s-suffrage-movements.sum: Movements to win women the right to vote succeeded country by country, between the 1890s and the late 20th century.

event/world-war-i.sum: World War I (1914 to 1918) was a global conflict, centered in Europe, that killed roughly 10 million soldiers and millions of civilians.

event/world-war-ii.sum: World War II (1939 to 1945) was a global conflict that killed an estimated 60 to 85 million people, estimates varying by source, including about six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust.

event/xinhai-revolution.sum: The Xinhai Revolution of 1911 to 1912 opened with an army mutiny at Wuchang and closed the Qing dynasty, which had ruled China since 1644, replacing imperial rule with the Republic of China.

event/younger-dryas.sum: The Younger Dryas was a sudden return of near-glacial cold across the Northern Hemisphere, lasting from about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, on the very threshold of the Holocene.

event/zanclean-flood.sum: The Zanclean flood: the refilling of the Mediterranean Sea by Atlantic water, through the Gibraltar region, about 5.33 million years ago. It ended the Messinian salinity crisis. It coincides with the start of the Pliocene.

observer-note/fire-then-everything.sum: Is there one change, one threshold, that best explains how the species rose so rapidly in power over other animals?

observer-note/frontiers-of-extraction.sum: What happens at the edge of a world economy when a distant demand meets a local resource?

observer-note/sanctioned-harm.sum: Why does a species with strong inhibitions against harming its own kind organize killing on a mass scale?

observer-note/second-chances-how-the-spe.sum: When two populations have no contact with each other but face the same problem, do they tend to reach the same solution?

observer-note/story-glue-how-strangers-c.sum: Most animals cooperate only with kin or with individuals they know personally. How, then, does one species build cooperation among millions of strangers who will never meet?

observer-note/the-fiction-of-claim-lines.sum: How can a line with no existence on the ground decide where millions of people live, work, and die?

observer-note/the-great-outsourcing-of-m.sum: Why does a species already gifted with a large, capable memory keep moving that memory outside its own body?

observer-note/the-settling-and-its-barga.sum: Why did foragers, who lived well enough without any farm, take up a way of life that so often looked worse for the person living it?

observer-note/the-species-as-a-geologica.sum: When does a species become a planetary process, and what does the record say about how such changes come to an end?

observer-note/who-writes-the-record.sum: How much of what is known about the past merely reflects the people who happened to write it down?

observer-note/why-the-species-buries-its.sum: Why does a species spend such great amounts of time, labor, and goods on bodies that can no longer work, fight, or bear young?
