place/bagan.sum: Bagan is an archaeological zone on the Irrawaddy River in central Myanmar, a plain crowded with thousands of Buddhist monuments like a field of stone flowers. It was the capital of the Pagan Kingdom from a traditional founding date of 849…

place/baghdad.sum: Baghdad is a city on the Tigris River in Iraq, founded in 762 CE by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur as a round capital, a circle drawn upon the land. For about five centuries it was the seat of the Abbasid caliphs and a leading center of…

place/beringia.sum: Beringia was the land region, including a broad land bridge, that joined northeastern Siberia and Alaska when sea levels were lower during the last ice age, a road laid bare by the withdrawn sea, and that later flooded to form the Bering…

place/borobudur.sum: Borobudur is a large Mahayana Buddhist monument in central Java, a mountain of stacked terraces raised around 800 CE under the Sailendra dynasty, and it is often described as the world's largest Buddhist temple.

place/botany-bay.sum: Botany Bay is an inlet on the coast of Sydney, Australia, where the Gweagal and Kamaygal peoples lived for thousands of years before James Cook landed there in 1770; yet the British colony of 1788 was founded not on its shores but nearby,…

place/bukhara.sum: Bukhara is a city in the Zarafshan oasis of Uzbekistan, green water in the dry lands: once a Sogdian trading city, then the capital of the Samanid dynasty, and for more than a thousand years a center of Islamic learning on the Silk Roads.

place/cahokia.sum: Cahokia was the largest city of the Mississippian culture, near present-day St. Louis, a city of raised earth that flourished from about 1050 to 1350 CE.

place/caral.sum: Caral is an ancient city in Peru's Supe Valley, occupied from about 2600 BCE, and one of the oldest known urban centers in the Americas, an early flame of city life in that land.

place/carthage.sum: Carthage was a Phoenician colony on the coast of present-day Tunisia, traditionally founded in 814 BCE, which grew into a major Mediterranean power, a queen of the western sea, until Rome destroyed it in 146 BCE.

place/chaco-canyon.sum: Chaco Canyon, in northwestern New Mexico, was the ceremonial and trade heart of the Ancestral Puebloan world from about 850 to 1150 CE, the hearth toward which that whole world turned the way flowers turn to the morning.

place/chauvet-cave.sum: Chauvet Cave, in the Ardeche region of southern France, holds some of the oldest known figurative paintings, laid on the stone by early Homo sapiens about 36,000 years ago, a herd of pigment waiting in the dark.

place/chichen-itza.sum: Chichen Itza is a major Maya-Toltec city on the Yucatan Peninsula that flourished from about 800 to 1100 CE, crowned by its stepped pyramid, El Castillo, which climbs toward the sky like a staircase built for the sun.

place/constantinople.sum: Constantinople was founded in 330 CE by Emperor Constantine on the site of Byzantium, and it stood as the capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire, a crown set between two seas, until the Ottoman conquest in 1453.

place/cusco.sum: Cusco is a city high in the Andes of southern Peru, at about 3,400 meters, which Inca tradition says was founded around 1200 CE and which served as the capital of the Inca Empire, a heart of stone among the peaks, until the Spanish took it…

place/cordoba.sum: Córdoba is a city on the Guadalquivir River in Andalusia, southern Spain, founded by Rome in the 2nd century BCE and best known as the capital of Muslim Iberia and of the Umayyad caliphate of Córdoba (929 to 1031), a lamp lit beside slow…

place/doggerland.sum: Doggerland was a lowland region of hunter-gatherers that joined Britain to continental Europe, lying where the North Sea is today. Then the seas rose. Gradually. Until the land was flooded.

place/elmina-castle.sum: Elmina Castle is a fortress on the coast of Ghana, built by the Portuguese in 1482 as São Jorge da Mina, the first European fort on the Gulf of Guinea, and later a holding place for people sold into the Atlantic slave trade. Its walls…

place/forbidden-city.sum: The Forbidden City is the former imperial palace complex at the heart of Beijing, China, built from 1406 to 1420 for the Ming dynasty and, until 1924, the residence and ceremonial center of Ming and Qing emperors, a walled sun around which…

place/ganges-river.sum: The Ganges River (Ganga) is a river of northern India and Bangladesh about 2,525 kilometers long, running from the Himalaya to the Bay of Bengal like a silver thread drawn from snow to sea; its plain has supported some of South Asia's…

place/giza-necropolis.sum: The Giza Necropolis, near Cairo, holds three large pyramids raised for the pharaohs Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure in the 26th century BCE, and beside them the Great Sphinx keeps its long vigil over the sand.

place/goree-island.sum: Gorée Island is a small island off Dakar, Senegal, held in turn by the Portuguese, Dutch, British and French from the 15th century, and it stands as a symbol of the Atlantic slave trade, though historians debate how many enslaved people…

place/great-wall-of-china.sum: The Great Wall of China is a series of walls, ditches, towers and forts built across northern China by successive states and dynasties from about the 7th century BCE to the 17th century CE, mainly to control movement between farming…

place/great-zimbabwe.sum: Great Zimbabwe was a large stone-walled capital city in southeastern Africa, occupied from about the 11th to 15th century CE, a crown of stone set upon the land and ancestral to the Shona-speaking peoples.

place/gobekli-tepe.sum: Göbekli Tepe is a Pre-Pottery Neolithic site in southeastern Turkey, dating to about 9500 to 8000 BCE, where large carved T-shaped stone pillars stand like a council of stone giants.

place/harappa.sum: Harappa is an archaeological site in Punjab, Pakistan, on a dry bed of the Ravi River, a riverbed the water has forgotten; occupied from about 3300 BCE, it was a major city of the Indus Valley Civilization until its urban phase declined…

place/hattusa.sum: Hattusa was the capital of the Hittite Empire, at Boğazkale in central Turkey, made the royal seat in about 1650 BCE and abandoned around 1200 BCE, and it preserved an archive of about 30,000 clay tablets, a memory of clay that outlasted…

place/hegra.sum: Hegra, also called Mada'in Salih, is an archaeological site in the AlUla region of northwestern Saudi Arabia, the second major city of the Nabataean kingdom after Petra, known for 111 monumental rock-cut tombs, doors hewn into the living…

place/hiroshima.sum: Hiroshima is a city on the delta of the Ōta River in western Honshu, Japan, founded as a castle town in 1589 and, on 6 August 1945, the first city struck by a nuclear weapon. Its history is older than that morning, but no honest account of…

place/hispaniola.sum: Hispaniola is the second-largest island of the Caribbean, in the Greater Antilles, one island divided into two sovereignties: Haiti in the west, the Dominican Republic in the east. Remember it also as a threshold, the site of the first…

place/isfahan.sum: Isfahan is a city on the Zayande River in central Iran, twice a capital: a Seljuk capital from 1051, and the capital of the Safavid Empire from 1598, when Shah Abbas I rebuilt its heart around the great square Naqsh-e Jahan, laid open like…

place/issyk-kul.sum: Issyk-Kul is a large mountain lake in the northern Tian Shan of Kyrgyzstan, held like a bowl of sky at about 1,600 meters above sea level. It lies on the routes between the steppe and the oases, near cemeteries whose graves have been…

place/jack-hills-zircons.sum: The Jack Hills zircons are tiny crystals from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, some dated to about 4.4 billion years: the oldest known pieces of Earth's crust, sparks that outlived the fire that struck them.

place/jamestown.sum: Jamestown, on the James River in Virginia, USA, was founded in 1607 as the first permanent English settlement in North America, and it remained the capital of the Virginia colony until 1699. Read it as a threshold, and read it whole.

place/jericho.sum: Jericho, at Tell es-Sultan in the Jordan Valley, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements, its permanent occupation beginning around 9000 BCE, a hearth that has not gone cold since.

place/jerusalem.sum: Jerusalem is a city in the Judean hills of the southern Levant, settled since about the 4th millennium BCE and holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims, a hill toward which many roads of faith run like water to a well. Its political status is…

place/karnak.sum: Karnak is a vast temple complex at Thebes, near modern Luxor in Egypt, dedicated mainly to the god Amun-Ra, and it grew like a reef over about 2,000 years, built and enlarged from the Middle Kingdom to the Ptolemaic period.

place/kilwa-kisiwani.sum: Kilwa Kisiwani is an island town off the coast of southern Tanzania, a leading Swahili port from about the 12th to the 15th century, where gold from the interior met goods carried across the Indian Ocean as river water meets the tide.

place/knossos.sum: Knossos is an archaeological site near Heraklion on the Greek island of Crete, occupied from about 7000 BCE, where the largest palace of the Minoan civilization rose from about 1900 BCE, a many-chambered crown upon the island.

place/kolyma.sum: Kolyma is a remote region of northeastern Siberia, Russia, that from 1932 until the 1950s held the Soviet Union's largest system of forced-labor camps, where prisoners mined gold and other metals in extreme cold and many died. We should…

place/kuk-early-agricultural-site.sum: The Kuk Early Agricultural Site in the highlands of Papua New Guinea keeps, like the lines on an old palm, drainage ditches and gardens showing that people cultivated wetlands there for at least 7,000 years.

place/l-anse-aux-meadows.sum: L'Anse aux Meadows is an archaeological site on the northern tip of Newfoundland, Canada, where Norse people from Greenland raised a small settlement of sod buildings around 1000 CE, a spark struck on a far shore: the only widely accepted…

place/lake-baikal.sum: Lake Baikal is a rift lake in southern Siberia, Russia, the deepest and oldest lake on Earth and the largest by volume of fresh water, a blue eye open on the world for ages; people have lived around it for many thousands of years, and…

place/lake-titicaca.sum: Lake Titicaca is a large high-altitude lake on the border of Peru and Bolivia, a mirror held up to the sky, sacred to the Inca as the birthplace of their first rulers and long settled by farming and fishing communities of the Andean…

place/library-of-alexandria.sum: The Library of Alexandria was a major research library in Ptolemaic Egypt, founded in the early 3rd century BCE as part of the Mouseion, and you should know this first: its decline was gradual rather than a single catastrophe.

place/london.sum: London is the capital of the United Kingdom, on the Thames River, founded as the Roman town of Londinium in about 47 CE. Like a river gathering its tributaries, it grew into a leading center of trade, finance and empire and, in the 19th…

place/machu-picchu.sum: Machu Picchu is a citadel of stone raised about 1450 among the Peruvian Andes, where the ridges break like frozen surf, and it was probably a royal estate for the Inca ruler Pachacuti.

place/marib.sum: Marib is a city in Yemen at the edge of the Ramlat al-Sabatayn desert, east of Sanaa, where sand meets sown ground. From about the 8th century BCE it was the capital of the Kingdom of Saba, and a great dam there once drank the floods and…

place/mausoleum-of-qin-shi-huang.sum: The Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang is the burial complex of the first emperor of unified China, laid near Xi'an in Shaanxi and begun in 246 BCE; east of its tomb mound, in buried pits, stands the Terracotta Army, a host of clay soldiers…

place/merv.sum: Merv was a great oasis city on the Silk Roads, in what is now Turkmenistan, a green jewel held in turn by many hands: a city of the Achaemenid Persians, a capital of the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun and of the Seljuk sultans, and then sacked…

place/mesa-verde.sum: Mesa Verde is a plateau in the Four Corners region of southwestern Colorado, USA, where Ancestral Puebloan farmers lived from about 550 CE until about 1300, and where, in the late 12th and 13th centuries, they set their cliff dwellings…

place/mexico-city.sum: Mexico City is the capital of Mexico, built by the Spanish after 1521 on the site of Tenochtitlan in the former Lake Texcoco, and today one of the largest cities in the Americas. Think of it as a palimpsest: a capital written over the…

place/mogao-caves.sum: The Mogao Caves are a honeycomb of Buddhist cave temples cut into a cliff near Dunhuang, in Gansu, China, begun by tradition in 366 CE and filled with murals and sculptures over about a thousand years, at a crossroads of the Silk Roads…

place/mohenjo-daro.sum: Mohenjo-daro was a great city of the Indus Valley Civilization in present-day Pakistan, a lattice of brick where people dwelt from about 2500 to 1900 BCE.

place/monte-alban.sum: Monte Alban was the hilltop capital of the Zapotec people, crowning the Oaxaca Valley of Mexico; it was founded around 500 BCE and abandoned by about 800 CE, when the wind had its summit back.

place/monte-verde.sum: Monte Verde is an archaeological site in southern Chile that, for decades, was considered the best evidence that people lived in South America about 14,500 years ago, before the Clovis culture of North America kindled its fires; now its…

place/nalanda.sum: Nalanda is an archaeological site in Bihar, India, the ruin of a Buddhist monastic university founded in about the 5th century CE, a lamp that drew students from across Asia until it was sacked around 1200.

place/nan-madol.sum: Nan Madol is a ruined city of artificial stone islets raised in a lagoon off Pohnpei, in the Federated States of Micronesia; from about the 12th century until around 1628 it was the ceremonial and political heart of the Saudeleur dynasty,…

place/nara.sum: Nara is a city in Japan's Kansai region that was the capital, then called Heijō-kyō, from 710 to 784 CE, an age in which the Japanese court drew Chinese models of city planning, writing and state Buddhism into its own ground, as a field…

place/nile-river.sum: The Nile River is a river of northeastern Africa about 6,650 kilometers long, flowing north to the Mediterranean like a green spine through the land; from about the 6th millennium BCE its annual flood fed farming and the states of Egypt…

place/paris.sum: Paris is the capital of France, on the Seine River. It grew from a settlement of the Gaulish Parisii on the Île de la Cité in about the 3rd century BCE into a Roman town, a medieval capital, a center of revolutions and one of Europe's…

place/pasargadae.sum: Pasargadae was the first capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in about 550 BCE on the high plateau of Fars in present-day Iran, under a wide sky, and it holds his tomb.

place/persepolis.sum: Persepolis was a ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire in southwestern Iran, begun around 518 BCE under Darius I and burned by Alexander the Great's army in 330 BCE. It rose like a crown of stone and ended in flame.

place/pompeii.sum: Pompeii was a Roman town on the Bay of Naples in Italy, founded in about the 7th century BCE and buried under volcanic ash and pumice when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE. A town. A mountain. Then the grey.

place/port-royal.sum: Port Royal was an English port town at the tip of the Palisadoes spit, at the entrance to Kingston Harbour, Jamaica. It grew after 1655 as a base for privateers and traders, and on 7 June 1692 an earthquake took about two-thirds of its…

place/potosi.sum: Potosi is a mining city in the Bolivian Andes, founded in 1545 beside the silver mountain Cerro Rico, whose output supplied Spanish and world trade for centuries. Think of it as the place where a mountain became a ledger.

place/poverty-point.sum: Poverty Point is a large earthwork complex in Louisiana, built by hunter-gatherer-fishers between about 1700 and 1100 BCE, its concentric ridges spreading like ripples held in earth and its huge mounds rising like the backs of sleeping…

place/rapa-nui.sum: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) is a remote Pacific island settled by Polynesians around 1200 CE, famous for nearly a thousand monumental stone statues called moai, a people of stone at the far end of the sea.

place/robben-island.sum: Robben Island is a small island in Table Bay, about 7 kilometers off Cape Town, South Africa, best known for the political prisoners held there under apartheid, including Nelson Mandela. From the 17th century to 1996 it served as a place…

place/rock-hewn-churches-of-lalibela.sum: The Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela are eleven churches carved down into volcanic rock in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, traditionally attributed to King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty in the early 13th century. They were drawn out of…

place/rome.sum: Rome, traditionally founded in 753 BCE, grew from a small city on the Tiber into the capital of an empire, and it remains a major city today, a river-born seed become a tree of stone.

place/samarkand.sum: Samarkand is a city in present-day Uzbekistan, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities of Central Asia and a leading crossroads of the Silk Roads, where the caravans met like rivers at a delta.

place/sarai.sum: Sarai was the capital of the Golden Horde, the western part of the Mongol Empire, on the lower Volga River in present-day southern Russia, founded around 1250 by Batu Khan and sacked by Timur in 1395. It rose from the steppe like a tent…

place/stonehenge.sum: Stonehenge is a monument of standing stones on Salisbury Plain in southern England, begun as a circular earthwork around 3000 BCE and rebuilt in stone over the next several centuries, a ring the land has worn like a crown.

place/taj-mahal.sum: The Taj Mahal is a white marble mausoleum in Agra, built from about 1632 to 1653 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. It is a grief-rite made into a moon of stone.

place/tenochtitlan.sum: Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztec Empire, founded on an island in Lake Texcoco in 1325 and destroyed after a siege in 1521, a city that sat upon the lake like a lotus of stone.

place/teotihuacan.sum: Teotihuacan was a huge planned city in the Valley of Mexico that flourished from about 100 BCE to 550 CE, home to the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, mountains raised by human hands.

place/tikal.sum: Tikal is a large Maya city in the rainforest of northern Guatemala, with traces of farming from about 1000 BCE and a dominant Classic-period kingdom whose rulers left inscriptions from the 3rd to the 9th century CE. After about 950 the…

place/timbuktu.sum: Timbuktu is a city in Mali on the southern edge of the Sahara that became a hub of the trans-Saharan trade and of Islamic scholarship, a lamp of learning set at the desert's shore.

place/uluru.sum: Uluru is a large sandstone inselberg in central Australia, an island of stone rising from the plain, sacred to the Anangu people, who have been bound to the site for more than 10,000 years and hold traditional custodianship of it today.

place/upano-valley-settlements.sum: The Upano Valley settlements are a network of ancient urban centers in the Ecuadorian Amazon, documented by lidar and reported in 2024, occupied from about 500 BCE for many centuries, cities that slept beneath the green.

place/ur.sum: Ur was a Sumerian city in southern Iraq, occupied from about 3800 BCE and abandoned around 500 BCE, known for its Great Ziggurat, its royal cemetery, and its role as the capital of the Third Dynasty of Ur about 2100 BCE. It lived long, and…

place/uruk.sum: Uruk was a Sumerian city in southern Mesopotamia and one of the first large cities in the world, at its peak around 3200 to 2900 BCE, one of the hearths where the long fire of cities was early kindled.

place/valley-of-the-kings.sum: The Valley of the Kings is a valley on the west bank of the Nile opposite Thebes, in Egypt, where pharaohs of the New Kingdom were buried in rock-cut tombs from about 1500 to 1070 BCE, their sleep hidden in the stone heart of the hills.

place/varanasi.sum: Varanasi, also called Benares or Kashi, is a city on the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh, India, where people have lived without a break since about the 8th century BCE. Like a lamp never allowed to go out, it stands as the most important Hindu…

place/venice.sum: Venice is a city raised on islands in a lagoon at the head of the Adriatic Sea in northeastern Italy, settled from about the 5th to 6th century CE. As an independent republic until 1797 it was a leading maritime and trading power of the…

place/xingu-garden-cities.sum: The Xingu garden cities are pre-Columbian settlements in the upper Xingu region of Brazil, dating from about 1200 to 1600 CE. Their plazas, roads and ditches, a pattern written into the land like veins in a leaf, were mapped by the…

place/catalhoyuk.sum: Çatalhöyük was a large Neolithic settlement in central Turkey, occupied from about 7100 to 5700 BCE, its houses packed together like the cells of a honeycomb and entered from the roof.

region/andes.sum: The Andes are the mountain spine of western South America. In their highlands and along their coasts, societies raised complex states without wheeled transport or a conventional writing system, as rivers carve their canyons with no chisel…

region/arabian-peninsula.sum: The Arabian Peninsula is a large, largely arid peninsula cradled between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf, a land of long dry distances. Across it ran a corridor for trade, and within it Islam had its origin.

region/caribbean-and-atlantic-world.sum: The Caribbean and Atlantic World is the Caribbean basin together with the Atlantic coasts of the Americas, Europe, and Africa, bound to one another from the 15th century by shipping, by trade, and by forced migration. When we say 'Atlantic…

region/central-asian-oases.sum: The Central Asian Oases are the river valleys and oasis cities strung between the steppe and the Iranian plateau like lamps along a dark road, Samarkand and Bukhara among them, and they served as hubs of the Silk Roads.

region/central-asian-steppe.sum: The Central Asian Steppe is the vast grassland belt across northern Eurasia, a sea of grass under an open sky. Its mounted pastoralists, riding like weather out of the horizon, shaped the history of every neighboring civilization.

region/east-asia.sum: East Asia gathers China, Korea, Japan and neighboring regions beneath one wide sky. There China's centralized state tradition has endured as among the longest continuous political traditions, a river that has kept to its bed across the…

region/europe.sum: Europe is the western peninsula of Eurasia, a ragged shore thrust out into the ocean. It gave ground to early farming societies, held the Roman Empire's northern provinces, and later bore the technologies and empires of the early modern…

region/iranian-plateau.sum: The Iranian Plateau is the highland region raised between Mesopotamia and South Asia like a great stone table. It was the heartland of Persian empires and a link in the chain of overland routes across Eurasia.

region/levant-and-anatolia.sum: The Levant and Anatolia are the eastern Mediterranean coast and the Turkish peninsula, a crossroads where the ways of Africa, Asia, and Europe meet like threads drawn into one knot. They were also a center of early farming.

region/mediterranean-basin.sum: The Mediterranean Basin is the sea and the coasts that ring it like a cupped hand. It was one of history's most connected zones, where trade, cultural exchange, and conflict passed across the water like tides.

region/mesoamerica.sum: Mesoamerica is the cultural region stretching from central Mexico to Central America, a world that kindled its own fires. Independently of the Old World it developed farming (maize, beans, squash), monumental cities, writing, and a…

region/mesopotamia.sum: Mesopotamia is the land between and around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, two waters holding a country between them, in present-day Iraq and parts of neighboring countries. It is a birthplace of cities and of writing, where memory…

region/nile-valley.sum: The Nile Valley is the narrow, fertile corridor of the Nile River through northeastern Africa, a green thread drawn through the desert, and home to one of the earliest states.

region/oceania.sum: Oceania gathers Australia, New Guinea, and the Pacific islands, scattered across the great water like embers on dark cloth. It holds both the oldest continuing cultures outside Africa and the last large landmasses settled by humans.

region/planet-wide.sum: Planet-wide is the region tag for events and processes that touch the whole Earth, or that belong to no single place, such as mass extinctions, climate shifts, and global exchange networks, tides that wash over every shore at once.

region/siberia-and-the-arctic.sum: Siberia and the Arctic are the northern lands of Asia from the Urals to the Pacific, and the Arctic coasts beyond, where cold and permafrost, like patient hands, shaped both human ways of life and the preservation of the past.

region/south-asia.sum: South Asia is the Indian subcontinent, a great land set like a jewel into the southern sea. It is home to one of the earliest urban civilizations and to major religious and mathematical traditions.

source/ayutthaya-kingdom-search-summarie.sum: The kingdom's founding in 1351, the various names given to it, its role in trade and its relations with France, and the fall of its capital on 7 April 1767.

source/barboni-et-al-2017-early-formatio.sum: A lunar zircon age of 4.51 Ga: uranium-lead and lutetium-hafnium data from Apollo 14 zircons require that the Moon had formed by 4.51 Ga, within the first 60 million years of the Solar System. The paper also reviews later estimates of 4.35…

source/bengal-famine-of-1943-search-summ.sum: The range of death-toll estimates, Sen's entitlement argument, the loss of Burmese rice imports, and the criticism aimed at Churchill and the War Cabinet's discussions.

source/bergstrom-et-al-2020-origins-of-p.sum: Genome sequencing of 27 ancient dogs points to a single origin distinct from any living wolf population, with a divergence estimated roughly 40,000 to 27,000 years ago.

source/blackpast-on-the-haitian-revoluti.sum: Independence declared on 1 January 1804, with Haiti described as the first country founded by formerly enslaved people and the first nation to abolish slavery permanently.

source/blackpast-on-the-sokoto-caliphate.sum: The Sokoto Caliphate's founding, its extent, and its dates.

source/blackpast-on-toussaint-louverture.sum: Birth in 1743, freedom gained before 1791, the 1801 constitution, arrest and deportation in 1802, and death on 7 April 1803.

source/bottke-and-norman-2017-the-late-h.sum: Basin ages drawn from Apollo samples cluster near 3.9 Ga, and there is debate over whether a spike in impacts actually occurred.

source/braddy-et-al-2008-giant-eurypteri.sum: The pincer of Jaekelopterus rhenaniae, from the Early Devonian of Germany, yields a body-size estimate of about 2.5 m.

source/brahmagupta-and-fibonacci-on-zero.sum: Brahmagupta set out rules for arithmetic with zero in 628 CE, and Fibonacci's Liber abaci of 1202 introduced Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe.

source/britannica-on-abd-al-malik.sum: Abd al-Malik's reign (685-705), the Dome of the Rock, Arabic set as the administrative language, and a reform of the coinage.

source/britannica-on-al-andalus.sum: The conquest of Iberia beginning in 711, the Cordoba emirate of 756 and caliphate of 929, and the fall of Granada in 1492.

source/britannica-on-al-khwarizmi.sum: Al-Khwarizmi's work at the House of Wisdom under al-Ma'mun, the origins of the words 'algebra' and 'algorithm', and Hindu-Arabic numerals.

source/britannica-on-angiosperm-paleobot.sum: The age of the oldest angiosperm pollen, the Hauterivian and Barremian ages of the Early Cretaceous, about 132.9 to 125 million years ago, and the 2013 report of angiosperm-like pollen of Middle Triassic age, about 247.2 to 242 million…

source/britannica-on-archaefructus.sum: Archaefructus, from the Yixian Formation in China, dated about 125 Ma.

source/britannica-on-aristotle.sum: Aristotle's dates (384-322 BCE), his two decades at Plato's Academy, his tutoring of Alexander, his work on Lesbos, and his founding of the Lyceum after 335 BCE.

source/britannica-on-bedrich-hrozny.sum: In 1915, Hrozny demonstrated that Hittite is Indo-European.

source/britannica-on-beringia.sum: Beringia served as an intermittent Pleistocene land connection between northeastern Asia and northwestern North America: the most recent one began to appear about 38,000 years ago, reached its greatest extent about 20,000 years ago, when…

source/britannica-on-carolingian-minuscu.sum: Carolingian minuscule stands as a clear script, established through Charlemagne's educational reforms and promoted by Alcuin.

source/britannica-on-chauvet-pont-d-arc.sum: The discovery in 1994 (Jean Clottes visited the cave on 29 December 1994), radiocarbon ages showing a majority of samples about 35,500 years old and a smaller group 30,000 to 31,000 years old, the UNESCO listing in 2014, and the replica's…

source/britannica-on-chichen-itza.sum: El Castillo's 365 steps — 91 on each of four stairways, plus the top platform — the equinox serpent shadow, the largest ball court in the Americas at 545 feet (about 166 m) long, and Chichen Itza's UNESCO listing in 1988.

source/britannica-on-christopher-dresser.sum: This source supports Dresser's birth and death dates, his years of study at the School of Design (1847-54), his 1855 professorship of artistic botany, his 1859 doctorate from Jena, and his book The Art of Decorative Design (1862).

source/britannica-on-continental-drift.sum: Wegener proposed a detailed theory of continental drift in 1912, which later found support from seafloor spreading (Harry Hess, in the early 1960s) and from plate tectonic theory, formulated by the late 1960s.

source/britannica-on-emperor-meiji.sum: Birth on 3 November 1852 at Kyoto, accession to the throne in 1867 after his father's death, the coronation ceremony and Charter Oath of Five Principles in 1868, the Meiji Constitution of 1889, and death on 30 July 1912 at age 59.

source/britannica-on-ferdinand-de-lessep.sum: The building of the Suez Canal (1859-69) under Ferdinand de Lesseps, its official inauguration on 17 November 1869, and the British government's purchase of the khedive's canal shares in 1875.

source/britannica-on-filippo-brunellesch.sum: Brunelleschi's rediscovery of linear perspective, about 1410 to 1415, Alberti's codification of it in 1435, the dome of Florence Cathedral (1420-36), and the patronage of the Medici bank.

source/britannica-on-hernan-cortes.sum: Hernan Cortes's overthrow of the Aztec empire, from 1519 to 1521, with Tenochtitlan taken on 13 August 1521.

source/britannica-on-hunayn-ibn-ishaq.sum: Hunayn ibn Ishaq (808-873) was an Arab scholar whose translations of Plato, Aristotle, Galen, and Hippocrates made Greek thought available to Arab scholars, carried in Arabic and, more often, Syriac versions.

source/britannica-on-khadijah.sum: This source corroborates that Khadija is considered the first person to believe in Muhammad's message, and that she died in 619, a few years before the Hijra to Medina.

source/britannica-on-kublai-khan.sum: Kublai Khan, who reigned 1260-94, stands as the fifth emperor of the Yuan (Mongol) dynasty, and completed the conquest of China in 1279.

source/britannica-on-malinche.sum: This source corroborates her role as interpreter and go-between for Cortes and the Aztec emperor Moctezuma II, the 1519 presentation of enslaved women at Tabasco, her bearing Cortes a son, Martin, and her later marriage to Juan Jaramillo.

source/britannica-on-menilek-ii.sum: Birth on 17 August 1844 at Ankober, kingship of Shewa (1865-89) followed by imperial reign from 1889 to 1913, imported firearms, an expansion of the empire nearly to its present borders, the victory over Italy at Adwa on 1 March 1896, and…

source/britannica-on-mount-everest.sum: The official 2020 China-Nepal height of 8,848.86 m.

source/britannica-on-sakoku.sum: The Edo (Tokugawa) period, 1603 to 1867, and its sakoku policy of self-isolation: Spain expelled in 1624, Portuguese ships forbidden in 1639, the Dutch and Chinese confined to Dejima Island at Nagasaki, Perry's arrival in 1853, and the…

source/britannica-on-savitribai-phule.sum: This source supports her birth and death dates and places, her marriage at nine, her being taught by Jyotirao Phule, the 1848 Bhidewada school, the harassment with stones, mud, and dung, and her death from plague after she ran a plague…

source/britannica-on-sesshu.sum: This source supports his birth and death dates and places, his training under Shūbun at Shōkoku-ji, his move to Yamaguchi under the Ōuchi, the name Sesshū, probably taken in 1466, and his trip to Ming China, where he held the First Seat at…

source/britannica-on-simon-bolivar.sum: Bolivar served as president of Gran Colombia (1819-30) and dictator of Peru (1823-26); he liberated New Granada (1819), Venezuela (1821), and Quito (1822), and, with the help of Jose de San Martin, Peru (1824) and Bolivia (1825); and he…

source/britannica-on-the-abbasid-calipha.sum: Abbasid rule, 750 to 1258, Baghdad's founding by al-Mansur in 762, the Mongol sack of 1258, and Buyid and Seljuk control of Baghdad.

source/britannica-on-the-battle-of-adwa.sum: The Battle of Adwa, on 1 March 1896 near Adwa in north-central Ethiopia: an Italian force of 14,500 men against an Ethiopian army of approximately 100,000, more than 6,000 killed within the Italian army (slightly more than half of them…

source/britannica-on-the-battle-of-auste.sum: The Battle of Austerlitz, on 2 December 1805, the first engagement of the War of the Third Coalition, in which Napoleon's 68,000 troops defeated almost 90,000 Russians and Austrians.

source/britannica-on-the-chola-dynasty.sum: The Chola line begins with Vijayalaya, who reigned about 850 to 870 and opened the conquest of Pallava territory, continues through Rajaraja I, who reigned 985 to 1014 and raised the Brihadishvara Temple at Tanjore (Thanjavur), and ends…

source/britannica-on-the-cold-war.sum: This entry moves through NATO's formation and the first Soviet atomic test, both in 1949, the Warsaw Pact of 1955, a Berlin crisis in 1961, the 1962 installation of Soviet missiles in Cuba, and the Soviet Union's collapse in 1991.

source/britannica-on-the-columbian-excha.sum: This entry covers Crosby's 1972 book, which divided the exchange into diseases, animals and plants, the fall of the population of the Americas by 50 to 95 percent by 1650, and the crops and animals it carried both ways: maize, potatoes,…

source/britannica-on-the-coronation-of-c.sum: This entry marks Pope Leo III's crowning of Charlemagne as emperor on 25 December 800, two days after Leo had cleared himself of the charges against him.

source/britannica-on-the-dutch-east-indi.sum: This entry traces the company's foundation in the Dutch Republic in 1602, its trade monopoly between the Cape of Good Hope and the Straits of Magellan, the renaming of Jacatra as Batavia in 1619, and the state's takeover of its debts and…

source/britannica-on-the-ediacaran-perio.sum: This entry names the Ediacara fauna, itself named after the Ediacara Hills of South Australia, and records an assemblage in the Avalon Zone of Newfoundland dated to 565 million years.

source/britannica-on-the-epic-of-gilgame.sum: This entry names the standard 12-tablet Gilgamesh, found by Hormuzd Rassam in Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh.

source/britannica-on-the-fall-of-constan.sum: This entry covers the 55-day siege ending on 29 May 1453 under Mehmed II, the artillery barrage that opened on 6 April, the cannon of the Hungarian gunsmith Urban, and Constantine XI's death in battle.

source/britannica-on-the-green-revolutio.sum: This entry covers Norman Borlaug's wheat program in the Mexican Agricultural Program, running from 1943, the development of the IR8 rice strain at the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines, India's 1966 import of Mexican…

source/britannica-on-the-haitian-revolut.sum: This entry covers the revolution of 1791 to 1804, independence declared on 1 January 1804, and France's 1825 recognition of Haiti in return for an indemnity of nearly 100 million francs, payable annually until 1887.

source/britannica-on-the-maya.sum: This entry covers the Classic Period, about 250 to 900 CE, the cities of Tikal and Calakmul, hieroglyphic writing, the Long Count calendar with its zero date in 3113 BCE, positional notation and the use of zero, and more than five million…

source/britannica-on-the-meiji-restorati.sum: This entry covers Perry's arrival in Edo Bay in 1853, the coup d'etat at Kyoto on 3 January 1868, the Charter Oath of April 1868, and the replacement of the domains by prefectures in 1871.

source/britannica-on-the-mongol-empire.sum: This entry covers the founding of the Mongol empire in 1206, when Temujin was elected Genghis Khan, and its greatest extent of some 9 million square miles (about 23 million km2), which made it the largest contiguous land empire in history.

source/britannica-on-the-napoleonic-wars.sum: This entry frames the Napoleonic Wars as a series of wars between Napoleonic France and other European powers that, together with the French Revolutionary wars, made up a 23-year period of recurrent conflict ending with the Battle of…

source/britannica-on-the-parsis.sum: This entry presents the Parsis as descendants of Persian Zoroastrians who emigrated to India to escape persecution by Muslims, arriving in the 8th century (the migration may have been as late as the 10th), and settling first at Diu before…

source/britannica-on-the-qing-dynasty.sum: This entry covers Qing rule from 1644 to 1911/12, the empire's extension to include Outer Mongolia, Tibet, Dzungaria, Turkistan and Nepal, and the growth of the population from some 150 million to 450 million.

source/britannica-on-the-rigveda.sum: This entry presents the Rigveda as the oldest of the sacred books of Hinduism, composed in an ancient form of Sanskrit about 1500 BCE in the Punjab region and preserved orally until it was written down about 300 BCE.

source/britannica-on-the-russian-revolut.sum: This entry covers the two revolutions of 1917 (February, March New Style, and October, November), Nicholas II's abdication on 15 March 1917, and the Bolshevik seizure of power that led to the creation of the Soviet Union.

source/britannica-on-the-scramble-for-af.sum: This entry covers the extent of European control of Africa (10 percent in the 1870s, about 90 percent by 1914, every present-day country except Ethiopia and Liberia) and the Berlin Conference, held 15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885.

source/britannica-on-the-song-dynasty.sum: This entry covers the Song dynasty (960-1279): the Northern Song, founded by Zhao Kuangyin with its capital at Kaifeng, and the Southern Song, with its capital at Lin'an (Hangzhou).

source/britannica-on-the-stockton-and-da.sum: This entry covers the opening run of the Stockton and Darlington Railway on 27 September 1825 (Darlington to Stockton at about 15 miles per hour), described as the first railway in the world to operate freight and passenger service with…

source/britannica-on-the-sugar-revolutio.sum: This entry states that the Sugar Revolution in Barbados had momentous social, economic and political consequences, as the island's elite turned to large sugarcane plantations cultivated by oppressed labourers.

source/britannica-on-the-taiping-rebelli.sum: This entry covers the Taiping Rebellion of 1850 to 1864, which ravaged 17 provinces and took an estimated 20 million lives, the capture of Nanjing in 1853 (renamed Tianjing), and Hong Xiuquan's suicide in June.

source/britannica-on-the-thirty-years-wa.sum: This entry covers the war of 1618 to 1648, conventionally dated from the revolt of the Protestant nobles of Bohemia and Austria against Ferdinand II in 1618, and its end with the Treaty of Westphalia, negotiated from 1644 at Munster and…

source/britannica-on-the-treaty-of-verdu.sum: This entry records the division of the Carolingian Empire among three sons of Louis I in August 843.

source/britannica-on-the-tunguska-event.sum: This entry covers the 30 June 1908 explosion (7:14 am, an airburst at 5 to 10 km altitude with no crater), an energy of as much as 15 megatons, trees felled radially for 15 to 30 km over some 2,000 square km, and Kulik's expeditions of…

source/britannica-on-timur.sum: This entry gives the birth year as 1336 at Kesh, dominion over Transoxania by the 1360s and proclamation as sovereign of the Chagatai line of khans about 1370, and death at Otrar in February 1405 while preparing an expedition to China.

source/britannica-on-vasco-da-gama.sum: This entry covers the departure from Lisbon on 8 July 1497, arrival at Santa Helena Bay on 7 November, the rounding of the Cape of Good Hope on 22 November, and arrival at Calicut on 20 May 1498.

source/british-museum-on-the-rosetta-sto.sum: This entry covers the 196 BCE decree, its 1799 discovery, British acquisition in 1801, and decipherment in 1822.

source/british-raj-search-summaries.sum: This entry covers the Government of India Act of 1858, the transfer from the East India Company to the Crown, the new offices in London and Calcutta, and the end of the Raj in 1947.

source/brumm-et-al-2021-sulawesi-warty-p.sum: This entry gives the minimum age, 45.5 thousand years, of the Leang Tedongnge painting.

source/cambridge-classics-on-the-deciphe.sum: This entry covers Ventris's 1952 decipherment, Chadwick's collaboration, and the Greek language of Linear B.

source/cambridge-world-history.sum: This entry describes a scholarly multi-volume world history running from earliest times to the present.

source/canadian-encyclopedia-on-the-thul.sum: This entry places Thule origin about 900 CE in Alaska, its spread across the Arctic to Greenland by the 12th century, and the near-absence of Dorset ancestry in Thule and Inuit samples.

source/cdc-on-the-1918-influenza-pandemi.sum: This entry covers one third of the world's population (about 500 million) infected, mortality estimates of 17.4 to 100 million, and reconstruction of the virus in 2005.

source/champa-search-summaries.sum: This entry covers the dating of Champa from 192 CE, its religious mix, the My Son temples, the capital at Vijaya, its fall in 1471, and the annexation of Panduranga in 1832.

source/clarke-et-al-2024-scottish-proven.sum: This entry places the Altar Stone's origin in the Orcadian Basin, at least 750 km from Stonehenge.

source/clarkson-et-al-2017-madjedbebe.sum: This entry covers luminescence dating of Madjedbebe rock shelter; its interpretation stays debated.

source/clarkson-et-al-2020-human-occupat.sum: This entry covers the Toba eruption at about 74 ka and continuous human occupation across the ash layer in India.

source/commonwealth-franchise-act-1902-p.sum: This entry covers women's federal vote and right to stand in Australia, along with its exclusions.

source/condron-and-winsor-2012-meltwater.sum: This entry covers the Younger Dryas timing (about 12,900-11,700 years ago) and the meltwater-driven AMOC weakening explanation.

source/conway-morris-and-caron-2012-pika.sum: This entry covers the redescription of Pikaia from 114 specimens, and reads it as a stem-group chordate.

source/demenocal-et-al-2000-african-humi.sum: This entry presents marine sediment-core evidence for an abrupt AHP onset (~14,800 cal BP) and termination (~5,500 cal BP), contrasted with the archaeological record's more gradual picture.

source/dirks-et-al-2017-homo-naledi-age.sum: This entry gives the dating of Homo naledi fossils to 236,000 to 335,000 years ago.

source/don-quijote-on-the-spanish-conque.sum: This entry covers Pizarro's arrival in 1532 during the Atahualpa-Huascar civil war and Atahualpa's capture at Cajamarca.

source/double-helix-and-human-genome-pro.sum: This entry covers Watson and Crick's 1953 double helix, made with crystallographic evidence from Rosalind Franklin shown to them via Maurice Wilkins; the Human Genome Project running from October 1990 to April 2003; and the 2022 complete…

source/durham-university-on-jericho.sum: This entry covers Kenyon's excavations (1952-58), plastered skulls, and the site's early occupation.

source/earth-magazine-on-the-discovery-o.sum: This entry covers the 1861 discovery of the feather and the London specimen skeleton in the Solnhofen limestone.

source/ebsco-on-the-neolithic-revolution.sum: This entry covers the Neolithic Revolution beginning about 12,000 years ago (11th millennium BP in the Fertile Crescent), independent centers, potato in the Andes, and declining early-farmer health.

source/ebsco-research-starters-on-cixi.sum: This entry covers Cixi's life (1835-1908), her regency from 1861, backing of the Boxers and war declaration of 21 June 1900, the New Policies, and the debate over her legacy.

source/ebsco-research-starters-on-cleopa.sum: This entry gives her birth as c. 69 BCE, death in 30 BCE, and her learning of Egyptian.

source/ebsco-research-starters-on-monte-.sum: This entry covers Monte Alban, established around 500 BCE as the capital of the Zapotec civilization on a hilltop above the Oaxaca Valley, the danzantes stone slabs with hieroglyphs, and UNESCO's 1987 World Heritage designation.

source/education-about-asia-on-han-xiong.sum: This entry covers the Xiongnu confederation, the heqin treaty system, and Han relations.

source/el-dorado-and-the-muisca-search-s.sum: This entry presents the El Dorado legend as a coronation ritual in which a new Muisca ruler, covered in gold dust, entered Lake Guatavita, and describes the Muisca as skilled goldsmiths who obtained gold largely by trade.

source/encyclopaedia-iranica-on-zoroaste.sum: This entry covers the debate over Zoroaster's date (consensus near 1000 BCE, with proposals from about 1750 BCE to the 6th century).

source/encyclopedia-of-the-enlightenment.sum: This entry covers the Encyclopedie, published 1751-1772 (17 text volumes by 1765, plates by 1772), The Wealth of Nations, published 9 March 1776, and Kant's essay of December 1784.

source/encyclopedia-com-on-potosi.sum: This entry covers silver discovered at Cerro Rico in 1545, amalgamation in the mid-1570s, Toledo's 1573 mita, and a population of about 160,000 by 1650.

source/encyclopedia-com-on-tupac-amaru-j.sum: This entry supports his descent from the Inca Túpac Amaru, executed by Toledo in 1572, the 10 November 1780 date of Arriaga's execution, the 18 May 1781 execution in Cusco, and the March 1738 birth date.

source/end-of-the-soviet-union-dates-sea.sum: This ledger of dates tracks the Soviet Union's unwinding: the Berlin border crossings opening on 9 November 1989, Gorbachev's perestroika running from 1986 and glasnost as a policy from 1985 to 1988, the hardliners' failed coup of 18 to 22…

source/engelman-2023-dunkleosteus-body-l.sum: This paper's revised length estimate puts typical adults at about 3.4 m and the largest individuals at about 4.1 m, replacing the older figures of 6 to 10 m.

source/english-wikipedia.sum: This entry stands in for English Wikipedia as a whole, whenever a note cites it without naming a specific article. No article was read under this title, so a check resting only on this note is not confirmed by any text actually read;…

source/facing-history-on-raphael-lemkin.sum: Lemkin coined the word 'genocide' in 1944; the UN Genocide Convention won approval on 9 December 1948.

source/first-fleet-mabo-and-aboriginal-l.sum: This gathers the High Court's Mabo (No 2) decision of 3 June 1992, which rejected terra nullius; the arrival of the First Fleet (its last ships reaching Botany Bay on 20 January 1788, with settlement at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788); and…

source/freidline-et-al-2023-tam-pa-ling.sum: Fossil evidence and Bayesian-modeled dating push the record of Homo sapiens in mainland Southeast Asia back to about 86,000-68,000 years ago.

source/fu-et-al-2025-harbin-denisovan-st.sum: This paper identifies the Harbin cranium as Denisovan.

source/garcia-castellanos-et-al-2009-med.sum: About 5.33 Ma, a catastrophic flood through Gibraltar refilled the Mediterranean.

source/gaunitz-et-al-2018-botai-horses.sum: Botai horses turn out to be ancestors of Przewalski's horses, not of modern domestic horses.

source/ghana-empire-search-summaries.sum: This covers the empire's location, its origins, the gold-salt trade, its capital, al-Bakri's description of it, the Almoravid sack of about 1076, and the decline that ended in absorption into Mali.

source/giaccio-et-al-2017-dating-the-cam.sum: This fixes a precise age for the Campanian Ignimbrite eruption, 39.85 ± 0.14 ka, synchronized against varve and ice-core chronologies.

source/global-nonviolent-action-database.sum: This supports that the Xapuri Rural Workers' Union was founded in 1977, with Chico Mendes playing a crucial organizing role alongside Marina Silva.

source/global-slavery-index-2023-walk-fr.sum: This estimates about 50 million people living in modern slavery in 2021 (49.6 million).

source/goren-inbar-et-al-2004-fire-at-ge.sum: Burned seeds, wood and flint at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov date to about 790,000 years ago.

source/green-et-al-2010-neandertal-genom.sum: This is the first Neanderthal genome, with evidence of gene flow into non-Africans of up to about 2 percent.

source/gross-and-zhao-2014-origins-of-do.sum: Japonica rice was domesticated in the Yangtze basin about 7,000 years ago; indica arose later through hybridization, from the wild ancestor Oryza rufipogon.

source/hacker-2011-civil-war-death-toll.sum: The traditional estimate holds about 620,000 Civil War dead; Hacker's census-based revision raises that to about 750,000, within a range of 650,000 to 850,000.

source/hays-et-al-1976-pacemaker-of-the-.sum: Deep-sea sediment evidence shows ice-age cycles following the orbital periods of eccentricity, tilt and precession.

source/heggarty-et-al-2023-indo-european.sum: This proposes a hybrid model: the Indo-European homeland lay south of the Caucasus, with a later branch moving north onto the steppe, feeding the Yamnaya and Corded Ware expansions into Europe.

source/henshilwood-et-al-2009-blombos-en.sum: The engraved ochre dates to about 75,000 to 100,000 years old.

source/hershkovitz-et-al-2018-misliya-ma.sum: A fossil upper jaw from Misliya Cave, Mount Carmel, Israel, dates to about 177,000 to 194,000 years ago, older than the previous oldest non-African fossils at Skhul and Qafzeh (about 90,000 to 120,000 years ago).

source/higham-et-al-2014-neanderthal-dis.sum: Radiocarbon dating across 40 sites places the end of the Mousterian at about 41,030 to 39,260 calibrated years before present, with an overlap with modern humans of about 2,600 to 5,400 years.

source/history-com-on-the-indian-removal.sum: The Act was signed on 28 May 1830; it names the five southeastern nations, the case Worcester v. Georgia (1832), and about 4,000 deaths among about 16,000 Cherokee in 1838.

source/hublin-et-al-2017-jebel-irhoud.sum: This describes and interprets the Jebel Irhoud fossils: a mosaic of facial, mandibular and dental features aligned with early or recent modern humans, alongside a more primitive braincase. It gives the site's age as 300 to 350 thousand…

source/hublin-et-al-2020-bacho-kiro-cave.sum: Homo sapiens fossils here date to about 46,000 to 44,000 years ago, among the earliest securely dated in Europe.

source/iasi-et-al-2024-neanderthal-ances.sum: This times most Neanderthal gene flow into modern humans to about 50,500 to 43,500 years ago, lasting about 7,000 years.

source/ics-international-chronostratigra.sum: This gives authoritative boundaries and names for geological eons, eras, periods and epochs.

source/internet-encyclopedia-of-philosop.sum: This covers Confucius (551-479 BCE): the Analects, ren, li and xiao, his lack of political success in his own life, the Han-era orthodoxy set under Emperor Wu, and the examination system.

source/ipcc-ar6-and-the-paris-agreement-.sum: This covers the AR6 Working Group I conclusion, from August 2021, that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land, and the Paris Agreement of 12 December 2015, with its goals of holding warming well…

source/ipcc-ar6-synthesis-report-2023.sum: This reports warming of about 1.1 degrees Celsius across 2011 to 2020, relative to 1850 to 1900.

source/wikipedia-on-twenty-fifth-dynasty.sum: This source backs the point that Kashta is sometimes counted as the dynasty's first pharaoh while Piye stands as the mainstream first ruler, and the dispute over the Shabaka and Shebitku succession.

source/wikipedia-on-tupac-amaru-ii.sum: This source backs his kuraka and muleteer background, his adoption of the name of Túpac Amaru I to claim Inca descent, and the birth year given as c. 1742.

source/wikipedia-on-todai-ji.sum: This source backs the 743 order, the 751 completion and 752 eye-opening ceremony of the Great Buddha, its 14.98 m height, and the Shōsōin's preservation of Tenpyō-period artifacts.

source/wikipedia-on-ur.sum: This source backs the site location, the c. 3800 BC to after 500 BC occupation span with its proposed causes of decline, Woolley's 1922-1934 excavation, the royal tombs c. 2600 BC, and the CT-scan evidence on the skulls.

source/wikipedia-on-uss-maine-acr-1.sum: This source backs the 15 February 1898 explosion in Havana harbor, the 268 sailors killed, and its contribution to the Spanish-American War.

source/wikipedia-on-vaballathus.sum: This source backs the 271-272 coinage pairing Vaballathus with Aurelian, and the subsequent adoption of the Augustus/Augusta titles.

source/wikipedia-on-valley-of-the-kings.sum: This source backs the burial period (c. 1539-1075 BC), the west-bank location opposite Thebes, the count of 65 tombs and chambers, the KV62 discovery in November 1922, and the 1979 UNESCO inscription.

source/wikipedia-on-varanasi.sum: This source backs the city's location on the left bank of the Ganges, the 800 BCE excavation finds, the ghats and cremation ghats, and the 2011 census populations.

source/wikipedia-on-vienna-secession.sum: This source backs the founding date of 3 April 1897 and Klimt as the first president of the Vienna Secession.

source/wikipedia-on-vietnamese-declarati.sum: This source backs the date, place (Ba Dinh Square, Hanoi) and authorship of the 2 September 1945 declaration.

source/wikipedia-on-vincent-van-gogh.sum: This source backs his birth, the shooting on 27 July and his death on 29 July 1890 at 37, the output figures of about 2,100 works and 860 oils, and the 1914 publication of the letters.

source/wikipedia-on-vitus-bering.sum: This source backs Bering's baptism date and place, his 1704 entry into the Russian navy, his death date and its disputed cause, the 1741 landfall at Mount Saint Elias, and the figures of 77 aboard and 46 surviving.

source/wikipedia-on-wangari-maathai.sum: This source backs her birth and death dates, the 1971 doctorate, the 1977 founding of the Green Belt Movement, the 2002 election and 2003 ministerial post, the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize, and the 2004 HIV dispute.

source/wikipedia-on-war-of-the-golden-st.sum: This source backs Hodgson's arrival in Kumasi on 25 March 1900 and his demand for the Golden Stool, the siege and relief of the fort on 15 July 1900, the 1901 exile of Yaa Asantewaa to the Seychelles, and the fact that the Golden Stool was…

source/wikipedia-on-wassily-kandinsky.sum: This source backs the birth and death dates and places, the 1896 move to Munich, Der Blaue Reiter in 1911, Bauhaus teaching from 1922 to 1933, French citizenship in 1939, and the Impressions, Improvisations and Compositions scheme.

source/wikipedia-on-wilfrid-laurier.sum: This source backs Laurier's birth and death dates, his Liberal leadership and premiership dates, his record 15-year term, the Boer War dispute with Quebec, and the 1911 reciprocity election defeat.

source/wikipedia-on-william-morris.sum: This source backs Morris's birth and death dates and places, the 1861 founding and 1875 reorganisation of his firm, the 1884 Socialist League, and the 1891 Kelmscott Press.

source/wikipedia-on-william-of-rubruck.sum: This source backs that Rubruck set out on a missionary journey on Louis IX's orders in 1253 and visited Karakorum in 1253-1254.

source/wikipedia-on-women-s-suffrage-in-.sum: This source backs the 19 September 1893 assent, the 28 November 1893 first women's vote, Māori women receiving the vote at the same time, the 1919 eligibility to stand, and New Zealand being the first nation where all women could vote in…

source/wikipedia-on-wu-ding.sum: This source backs the c. 1250 to 1192 BC dating of Wu Ding's reign, and notes that other chronologies differ.

source/wikipedia-on-wu-school.sum: This source backs the statement that Shen Zhou is usually cited as the founder of the Wu School, a loose group of Ming literati painters united by shared artistic theories.

source/wikipedia-on-xi-an-stele.sum: This source backs the erection of the Christian stele at Chang'an on 4 February 781 and its record of early Christianity in China.

source/wikipedia-on-xuanzang.sum: This source backs his birth and death dates, the 627 or 629 departure against a travel ban, the 645 return and welcome by Emperor Taizong, and the Journey to the West link.

source/wikipedia-on-yaa-asantewaa.sum: This source backs her birth around 1840, her role as Queen Mother of Ejisu, the 1896 exile of Prempeh I, the March 1900 siege of Kumasi fort, her death in exile in the Seychelles on 17 October 1921, and the 1 January 1902 annexation.

source/wikipedia-on-yellow-river.sum: This source backs the river's length, source and mouth, its silt load and raised bed at Kaifeng, its flood and course-change counts, the southern course period, and the 1887 and 1938 death-toll estimates.

source/wikipedia-on-yermak-timofeyevich.sum: This entry backs Yermak's life dates (c. 1532 to 5 or 6 August 1585): the 840-man force, the October 1582 capture of Qashliq, the tsar's pardon and gifts, the ambush that killed him and the legend that he drowned, and the founding of…

source/wikipedia-on-yongle-emperor.sum: This source backs Zhu Di's birth, death and reign dates, the 1399-1402 civil war, the succession background, the capital move to Beijing, and the count and reach of Zheng He's voyages.

source/wikipedia-on-zenobia.sum: This entry backs Odaenathus's assassination c.267, Zenobia's regency for Vaballathus, the 270-271 conquest of Egypt and Anatolia, the 272 battles of Immae and Emesa, and her capture near the Euphrates.

source/willeit-et-al-2019-mid-pleistocen.sum: One modeled explanation of why glacial cycles stretched from about 41,000 years to about 100,000 years.

source/woese-and-fox-1977-prokaryotic-do.sum: The 1977 ribosomal RNA evidence showing that methane-producing microbes form a lineage distinct from both bacteria and eukaryotes — the foundation of the domain Archaea.

source/world-history-encyclopedia-on-bor.sum: Built across the 8th and 9th centuries under the Sailendra, the monument carries 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddha statues; it was rediscovered in 1814 and inscribed by UNESCO in 1991.

source/world-history-encyclopedia-on-car.sum: The traditional founding of Carthage from Tyre in 814 BCE, the 22-letter Phoenician alphabet, and purple dye drawn from murex.

source/world-history-encyclopedia-on-cyr.sum: An uncertain birth date, the capture of Astyages in 550 BCE, the conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE, death in 530 BCE, and the tomb at Pasargadae.

source/world-history-encyclopedia-on-gra.sum: Grave Circle A at Mycenae, dated to about 1600 BCE, and Schliemann's excavation of it in 1876.

source/world-history-encyclopedia-on-kin.sum: The Old Kingdom (c. 2613-2181 BCE), the Middle Kingdom (2040-1782), the New Kingdom (c. 1570-1069), the intermediate periods between them, and Egypt's transition to a Roman province in 30 BCE.

source/world-history-encyclopedia-on-mar.sum: The Ninety-five Theses in October 1517, the door-nailing story that is itself doubtful, the Diet of Worms in 1521, the New Testament of 1522, and the complete Bible of 1534.

source/world-history-encyclopedia-on-nar.sum: Unification traditionally dated to about 3100 BCE, the identification of Narmer with Menes, the two crowns shown on the palette, and the view that unification was gradual and only complete under Khasekhemwy (c. 2680 BCE).

source/world-history-encyclopedia-on-pol.sum: Double-hulled canoes, navigation without instruments, and the Lapita ancestors who reached Remote Oceania between about 1300 and 900 BCE.

source/world-history-encyclopedia-on-sid.sum: The traditional dates (c. 563-483 BCE), later scholarly dates (death between about 411 and 400 BCE, life c. 480-400 BCE), and the awakening at Bodh Gaya.

source/world-history-encyclopedia-on-sum.sum: The Sumerian city-states of Eridu, Uruk, Ur and Lagash, the cuneiform script, and Sumerian's standing as a language isolate.

source/world-history-encyclopedia-on-the.sum: The battle of Actium on 2 September 31 BCE, and Cleopatra's alliance with Antony.

source/world-history-encyclopedia-on-zor.sum: Zoroastrianism's standing as the state religion of the Sasanian Empire, 224-651 CE.

source/world-history-encyclopedia.sum: Ibn Battuta's travels, and how the Rihla came to be written.

source/wu-et-al-2012-xianrendong-pottery.sum: The age of the earliest known pottery.

source/xinhai-revolution-search-summarie.sum: The Wuchang Uprising on 10 October 1911, Puyi's abdication on 12 February 1912, and the compromise reached between Sun Yat-sen and Yuan Shikai.

source/zagwe-dynasty-search-summaries.sum: The Zagwe span, about 1137 to 1270, Lalibela's reign, the eleven rock-hewn churches, and the Solomonic claim made by the dynasty that followed.

source/zaremba-niedzwiedzka-et-al-2017-a.sum: The Asgard archaea's standing as the closest archaeal relatives of eukaryotes.

source/zhu-et-al-2018-shangchen-stone-to.sum: Stone tools at Shangchen, dated from about 2.1 to 1.3 million years ago — the oldest evidence of hominins outside Africa.

species/cyanobacteria.sum: Cyanobacteria are bacteria that perform oxygen-producing photosynthesis, drinking sunlight and breathing out oxygen. Their work, breath upon breath, led to the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere, and the sky itself was changed.

species/denisovans.sum: Denisovans are an extinct human group, known first not by a face but by DNA, drawn from a finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia in 2010.

species/dinosaurs.sum: Dinosaurs were a diverse group of reptiles that dominated the land's ecosystems for about 165 million years, lords of a long age. Birds are living descendants of one dinosaur lineage, and so the old line still sings at the window.

species/ediacaran-biota.sum: The Ediacaran biota are the first large, complex, multicellular organisms in the fossil record, a strange early bloom beneath the waves, living in the sea in the last stretch of the Proterozoic, before the Cambrian.

species/flowering-plants.sum: Flowering plants (angiosperms) appear in the fossil record in the Early Cretaceous, about 130 million years ago, opening like a late dawn across the land, and now make up most land plant species.

species/homo-erectus.sum: Homo erectus was an early human species that endured from about 1.9 million to roughly 110,000 years ago, the first known hominin to spread widely beyond Africa, a wanderer who carried the old home outward.

species/homo-floresiensis.sum: Homo floresiensis, nicknamed 'the hobbit', was a small-bodied human species that lived on the Indonesian island of Flores, a people kept apart by the sea. Its bones date to about 100,000 to 60,000 years ago, and stone tools attributed to…

species/homo-habilis.sum: Homo habilis ('handy man'), a name that honors the hand, is an early member of the genus Homo that lived in Africa from about 2.4 to 1.4 million years ago.

species/homo-naledi.sum: Homo naledi is a small-brained human relative whose remains were found in the Rising Star cave system in South Africa in 2013, deep in the dark, and dated to about 335,000 to 236,000 years ago.

species/homo-neanderthalensis.sum: Neanderthals were a human species that dwelt in Europe and western Asia from about 400,000 to about 40,000 years ago, folk shaped for the cold, and they interbred with Homo sapiens.

species/homo-sapiens.sum: Homo sapiens is the species of modern humans: the only living member of the genus Homo, which emerged in Africa about 300,000 years ago and now numbers about eight billion, a single hearth grown into a sea of lamps.

species/pikaia.sum: Pikaia is a small, eel-like swimming animal from the Burgess Shale of British Columbia, about 505 million years old, a ribbon of life that once flickered through Cambrian water. Reinterpreted in 1979 as an early chordate, it is often cited…

species/rice.sum: Rice is a cereal grass domesticated from a wild ancestor in the Yangtze valley of China from about 9,000 years ago. It is now the staple food of more than half the world's population, as if a river's patience had been poured into a single…

species/sahelanthropus-tchadensis.sum: Sahelanthropus tchadensis is a roughly 7-million-year-old fossil ape from Chad, proposed as one of the earliest members of the human lineage, a figure standing at the far edge of the family's memory.

species/sorghum.sum: Sorghum is a drought-tolerant cereal grass domesticated in eastern Sudan more than 5,000 years ago, a grain that learned to live with thirst, and it remains a staple food across Africa, Central America and South Asia today.

species/soybean.sum: The soybean is a legume domesticated between the Yellow and Huai rivers in China between roughly 9,000 and 6,000 years ago. For a long time it was food, central to East Asian diets through tofu and soy sauce; now it is grown worldwide…

species/sponges.sum: Sponges (phylum Porifera) are simple aquatic animals without true tissues or organs, among the earliest branches of the animal family tree, still as stones in the water and yet alive. Unambiguous fossils begin in the earliest Cambrian,…

species/stromatolites.sum: Stromatolites are layered rock structures raised by communities of microbes that trap sediment and precipitate minerals, books of stone written one thin page at a time; the oldest widely cited examples are about 3.48 billion years old.

species/tea-plant.sum: The tea plant is native to the borderlands of southwestern China, northeastern India and northern Myanmar, and in China its leaves were drunk by at least the 2nd century BCE. Later its trade ran across the world like water finding every…

species/tiktaalik.sum: Tiktaalik is a 375-million-year-old fossil fish with limb-like fins and a flexible neck, a transitional form standing at the water's edge between fishes and four-limbed animals.

species/tobacco.sum: Tobacco is a plant native to the Americas, cultivated there since at least the 2nd millennium BCE and held in ceremony by many Indigenous peoples, like smoke rising between earth and sky. Spanish colonizers carried it to Europe in the 16th…

species/trilobites.sum: Trilobites were marine arthropods armored in a hard, segmented exoskeleton, and they thrived for about 270 million years, from the early Cambrian until the end-Permian extinction closed their long reign.

species/wheat.sum: Wheat is a cereal grass domesticated from wild einkorn and emmer in the Fertile Crescent from about 9600 BCE, and now it is grown on more land than any other food plant on Earth, a golden sea laid across the world's fields.

species/woolly-mammoth.sum: The woolly mammoth was a cold-adapted elephant of the northern Ice Age steppe, a shaggy lord of the frozen grasslands, which survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago, long after its kin had gone.

technology/airplane.sum: In 1903, a powered fixed-wing aircraft achieved documented, sustained, controlled flight with a pilot aboard, through the work of Orville and Wilbur Wright.

technology/alphabet.sum: The alphabet is a writing system in which signs stand for individual sounds. The first alphabet, Proto-Sinaitic, appeared around 1800 BCE and gave rise to most of the alphabets in use today.

technology/anesthesia.sum: Anesthesia is the use of drugs or vapors to block pain and consciousness during surgery. General anesthesia spread rapidly around the world after a public ether demonstration in 1846.

technology/antibiotics.sum: Antibiotics are drugs that kill or inhibit bacteria, and their story turns on a threshold: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, and mass production began in the 1940s.

technology/antikythera-mechanism.sum: The Antikythera Mechanism is a hand-cranked bronze device of gears, recovered from a shipwreck off Antikythera, Greece. It modeled the cycles of the moon and sun and predicted eclipses, and it remains the most intricate geared device known…

technology/astrolabe.sum: The astrolabe is an astronomical instrument that maps the celestial sphere onto a flat plate, letting its user tell time, find direction, and make astronomical observations. Its underlying mathematics took shape in Hellenistic Greek…

technology/battery.sum: A battery stores chemical energy and releases it as a steady electric current. The first practical version, Alessandro Volta's voltaic pile, was announced in 1800, opening the era of electricity on demand.

technology/bessemer-process.sum: The Bessemer process converts molten pig iron into steel by blowing air through it to burn off impurities, cutting production costs sharply. Henry Bessemer patented and announced it in England in 1856; the American ironmaster William Kelly…

technology/brewing-and-fermentation.sum: Brewing and fermentation use yeasts to turn the sugars in grain, honey, and fruit into alcohol. Residues found in pottery from Jiahu in China, dated to about 7000 to 6600 BCE, mark the earliest confirmed alcoholic drink.

technology/bronze-metallurgy.sum: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin -- or another metal -- first produced widely in the Near East around 3300 BCE, giving its name to the Bronze Age.

technology/calendars.sum: Calendars are systems for counting days and grouping them into months and years, usually by following the Sun, the Moon, or both. Egypt's 365-day civil calendar, in use by about 2500 BCE at the latest, ranks among the earliest.

technology/cannon.sum: A cannon is a metal-barreled weapon that fires a projectile using gunpowder's explosive force. It is first attested in China, and it spread across Eurasia over the following decades.

technology/chariot.sum: The chariot is a light, two-wheeled vehicle drawn by horses, used in war and in racing. The earliest known spoke-wheeled chariots come from Sintashta burials in the southern Urals, about 2000 BCE, though where the design actually began is…

technology/chinampas.sum: Chinampas are raised-bed farming plots built up within the shallow lake water of the Basin of Mexico, framed with woven fencing packed with mud and sediment. Highly fertile, they yielded multiple harvests a year and became a key food…

technology/code-of-hammurabi.sum: The Code of Hammurabi is a black stone stele inscribed in Akkadian cuneiform with about 282 laws, made for Hammurabi of Babylon around 1754 BCE. It was found at Susa in 1901-02 and now stands in the Louvre.

technology/codex.sum: The codex is the bound, page-based book format that replaced the papyrus scroll across the Mediterranean world from the 1st century CE onward, and it let writers use both sides of a page.

technology/coinage.sum: Coinage is the issue of stamped metal pieces of standard weight and value. The earliest known coins are electrum pieces from Lydia, found in a temple deposit at Ephesus dated to about 625 to 600 BCE; China and India each developed coin…

technology/crossbow.sum: The crossbow is a bow mounted on a stock, with a trigger holding the string drawn until release. The earliest known bronze trigger mechanisms come from Chu tombs in China, about the 5th century BCE, and Greek makers built a comparable…

technology/crucible-steel.sum: Crucible steel is high-carbon steel made by melting iron together with carbon-bearing material in a sealed clay crucible. The earliest confirmed production sites lie in South India, such as Kodumanal in Tamil Nadu, dated to about the 3rd…

technology/cyrus-cylinder.sum: The Cyrus Cylinder is a baked clay cylinder inscribed in cuneiform after Cyrus the Great's conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE. It was found at Babylon in 1879 and now stands in the British Museum.

technology/dead-sea-scrolls.sum: The Dead Sea Scrolls number roughly 900 ancient Jewish manuscripts, found in caves near Qumran by the Dead Sea, dating from about the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE.

technology/digital-computer.sum: The digital computer is a programmable machine that processes information as binary numbers. The ENIAC was completed in 1945, following earlier machines such as Zuse's Z3 (1941) and Colossus (1943).

technology/double-entry-bookkeeping.sum: Double-entry bookkeeping records each transaction as a matched debit in one account and a credit in another, keeping the books balanced and letting merchants track assets, liabilities, and profit. It appears in Italian trade cities by the…

technology/electric-lighting.sum: Practical incandescent lighting emerged from parallel work in Britain and the United States between 1878 and 1880, and it spread from there into homes and workplaces.

technology/electric-motor.sum: The electric motor turns electrical current into continuous mechanical rotation by way of electromagnetism. It developed in stages from 1821 to the late 1830s, moving from a bare demonstration of motion to machines producing usable work.

technology/electrical-power-grid.sum: Electrical power grids distribute electricity from central generators out to homes and factories. Thomas Edison opened the first commercial power station in New York in 1882.

technology/eyeglasses.sum: Think of eyeglasses as a simple architecture built from glass and metal: corrective lenses held in a frame across the eyes. The device first appears in northern Italy in the late 13th century, then spreads across Europe within decades,…

technology/gunpowder.sum: Gunpowder is a mix of saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal, discovered in China around the 9th century and turned into a military technology under the Song.
