technology/haber-bosch-process.sum: The Haber-Bosch process combines nitrogen from the air with hydrogen, under high pressure and over a catalyst, to make ammonia. Developed in Germany between 1908 and 1913, it underpins the whole architecture of synthetic nitrogen…

technology/insulin.sum: Insulin is a pancreatic hormone that regulates blood sugar. Before a Toronto team purified it across 1921 and 1922, type 1 diabetes was fatal, often within a year or two of diagnosis.

technology/internal-combustion-engine.sum: An internal combustion engine burns its fuel inside its own cylinder, so the expanding gas drives the piston directly, with no external boiler standing between them the way a steam engine needs.

technology/iron-smelting.sum: Iron smelting, the extraction of iron from ore, began on a limited scale in Anatolia in the early 2nd millennium BCE, possibly earlier, before becoming widespread across the Near East from the late 2nd millennium BCE, about 1200 BCE…

technology/irrigation-canals.sum: Irrigation canals are channels built to carry river water to fields. The earliest known examples sit at Choga Mami in Iraq, dated to about the 6th millennium BCE, and canal systems later supported southern Mesopotamian cities as well as…

technology/magnetic-compass.sum: The magnetic compass came into use for navigation at sea in China by about the 12th century, after an earlier life in divination, and reached Europe not long after.

technology/mechanical-clock.sum: Mechanical clocks, driven by falling weights and governed by an escapement, appeared in European towns and monasteries around 1300, after earlier Chinese and Islamic water clocks had already kept time by other means.

technology/microscope.sum: A microscope is an optical instrument built to magnify objects too small for the unaided eye. Compound microscopes appeared in the Netherlands around 1620, and single-lens designs later reached even higher magnification still.

technology/movable-type-printing-press.sum: The movable-type printing press, developed by Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz around 1440, let books be made quickly and cheaply across Europe.

technology/nuclear-fission.sum: Nuclear fission, the splitting of heavy atomic nuclei, was discovered by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in December 1938, and then explained by Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch.

technology/oldowan-stone-tools.sum: Oldowan tools are the earliest widespread stone tools: simple flakes and choppers made by striking one cobble against another, dating from about 2.6 million years ago.

technology/outrigger-canoe.sum: An outrigger canoe is a narrow hull steadied by a float lashed to one or both sides. Austronesian-speaking seafarers developed it, and its early use is dated here to the Lapita expansion of about 1600 BCE, mainly on indirect evidence.

technology/paper-money.sum: Jiaozi — paper notes issued by private merchants in Chengdu, Sichuan — appeared in the late 10th century as a lighter alternative to heavy iron coin. The Song Dynasty government took over their issuance in the 1020s, usually called the…

technology/paper.sum: Paper was developed in China around the 2nd century BCE to the 2nd century CE, and spread across Asia before reaching Europe by the 12th century.

technology/papyrus.sum: Papyrus is a writing material made from strips of the papyrus plant, first used in Egypt. A blank roll from the tomb of Hemaka at Saqqara dates to about 2900 BCE, while the oldest inscribed papyri, from Wadi al-Jarf, date to about 2560 BCE.

technology/photography.sum: Photography is the process of fixing an image cast by light onto a treated surface, developed in Europe through several overlapping methods across the early 19th century.

technology/porcelain.sum: Porcelain is a hard, white, translucent ceramic made by firing kaolin clay at very high temperature. Developed in China, it went on to become one of history's most widely traded manufactured goods.

technology/pottery.sum: Pottery — fired clay containers — appeared in East Asia at least 20,000 years ago, well before farming, and only later became widespread in the Neolithic.

technology/qanat.sum: A qanat is an underground channel that carries groundwater by gravity from a water-bearing slope down to fields, reached along its length by a line of vertical shafts. The earliest written record is an Assyrian account of 714 BCE…

technology/quipu.sum: A quipu, or khipu, is a recording device made of knotted cords, used across the Andes and best known from the Inca Empire.

technology/radio.sum: Radio is signaling by electromagnetic waves, without any wire between sender and receiver. Practical wireless telegraphy emerged in the 1890s out of several experimenters' work, and grew from there into ship communication, broadcasting,…

technology/railways.sum: Railways run by steam locomotives began with the Stockton and Darlington Railway in England in 1825, and went on to reshape transport, trade, and the experience of time across the 19th century.

technology/refrigeration.sum: Refrigeration is engineered cooling used to preserve food and other perishables. It moved from an 1834 lab-scale prototype to reliable industrial compression systems, taken up by brewers, meatpackers, and shippers between the 1850s and the…

technology/rosetta-stone.sum: The Rosetta Stone is a stele inscribed in 196 BCE with a decree written in Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Greek. Its discovery in 1799 is what allowed Egyptian hieroglyphs to finally be deciphered.

technology/sanitation-and-sewers.sum: Every settlement keeps a covenant with its own waste: carry it away, or live beside it. Sanitation and sewers are the architecture that keeps that covenant, the systems carrying waste water and human waste away from where people live. The…

technology/seismoscope.sum: A bronze instrument credited to Zhang Heng, court astronomer of the Han dynasty, said to detect the direction of a distant earthquake by letting a ball drop from a dragon's mouth into a toad's waiting mouth below.

technology/sericulture.sum: Sericulture is the raising of silkworms toward one end: silk thread. It began in China, where silk fragments from Qianshanyang in Zhejiang date to about 2700 BCE, and silk went on to become a leading good of Eurasian trade and diplomacy.

technology/steam-engine.sum: The steam engine is an architecture for converting heat into mechanical work. Thomas Newcomen built the first commercially successful engine in 1712, and James Watt's improvements, beginning in the 1760s, made it far more efficient.

technology/stirrup.sum: The stirrup is a foot support hung from a saddle, an architecture of mounting and balance. The earliest firm evidence is a single mounting stirrup shown on a Chinese figurine of about 302 CE, with paired stirrups following within decades.

technology/telegraph-and-submarine-cable.sum: The electric telegraph, first demonstrated commercially in the 1840s, and the submarine cables that followed it, built an architecture letting messages cross continents and oceans in minutes rather than weeks.

technology/telephone.sum: The telephone carries speech as electrical signals over wire. Alexander Graham Bell received the first US telephone patent in 1876, amid competing claims from other inventors.

technology/telescope.sum: The telescope is an optical instrument, an architecture of lenses built to magnify distant objects, first documented in the Netherlands in 1608 and turned toward the night sky soon after.

technology/terracotta-army.sum: The Terracotta Army is a buried architecture of life-size clay soldiers, horses, and chariots, raised for the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, first emperor of unified China, and left undiscovered until 1974.

technology/the-wheel.sum: Wheeled vehicles enter the archaeological record around 3500 to 3000 BCE, across Mesopotamia, Europe, and the steppe alike.

technology/trans-siberian-railway.sum: The Trans-Siberian Railway, begun in 1891 and largely complete by 1916, is an architecture of rail running about 9,300 kilometers, linking Moscow to the Pacific port of Vladivostok.

technology/vaccination.sum: Vaccination began in 1796, when Edward Jenner showed that cowpox inoculation could protect against smallpox, a discovery that led, in time, to the eradication of smallpox in 1980.

technology/variolation.sum: Variolation is deliberate exposure to smallpox material itself, whether by scratching the skin or by nasal insufflation of dried scab powder, meant to induce a milder infection and lasting immunity, and used before Jennerian vaccination.

technology/water-clock.sum: A water clock, or clepsydra, measures time by the steady flow of water into or out of a vessel. The oldest surviving example, the alabaster clepsydra from Karnak, was made in the reign of Amenhotep III in the 14th century BCE, though a…

technology/windmill.sum: The windmill is an architecture converting wind into rotational mechanical power, used historically to grind grain and pump water. The earliest well-documented windmills are the vertical-axis panemone mills of Sistan, on the Iranian…

technology/woodblock-printing.sum: Woodblock printing, the architecture of carving a whole page into a block of wood, inking it, and pressing it onto paper, took shape in East Asia by the 8th century CE.

technology/x-ray-imaging.sum: X-rays are penetrating electromagnetic radiation, identified in 1895 by Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen. Within months, they let physicians see bones and foreign objects inside a living body without any surgery at all.

technology/zero-and-place-value-notation.sum: The decimal place-value system, an architecture in which zero serves as both digit and placeholder, developed in India during the first millennium CE and spread from there across the world.

theme/trade-and-economy.sum: Trade and economy cover the production, exchange, and taxation of goods, labor, and money, and the institutions built to organize them: markets, credit, coinage, companies, tribute, and forced labor. This hub traces exchange from the…

theme/war-and-conflict.sum: War and conflict are organized violence between groups: raids, battles and sieges, conquests, rebellions, civil wars, and genocides, together with the treaties and settlements that bring them to an end. This hub follows them from the…

timeline/human-timeline.sum: The Human Timeline keeps the last 300,000 years: the origin of Homo sapiens, the prehistoric dispersals, the early states, the world religions, the empires, and at last the modern era, each age laid down upon the one before like layers of…

timeline/master-timeline.sum: The Master Timeline sets every era and event in the vault in chronological order, one long procession that runs from the formation of the Solar System to the present.
